cards.body: Use w-25, w-50, w-75, w-100 and w-auto for width, and h-25 to h-100 for height. Inside flex and grid containers, .gap-* adds space between items.

quiz.question: What does the class mt-3 do?
quiz.explanation: mt-* is margin-top; the number 3 means 1rem of space.

cards.title: Text Utilities
cards.body: text-center centres text, text-start aligns to the start and text-end aligns to the end. Text colours use text-primary, text-success, text-danger, text-muted and so on. Other helpers: fw-bold, fst-italic, text-uppercase and fs-1 to fs-6 for font size.

cards.title: Background Colours
cards.body: Use bg-primary, bg-success, bg-danger, bg-warning, bg-light and bg-dark for background colours. Pair a dark background with a light text colour (e.g. bg-dark text-white) for good contrast.

cards.title: Borders, Rounded Corners & Shadows
cards.body: Add a border with .border (or .border-top, .border-primary), round corners with .rounded or .rounded-circle, and add depth with .shadow, .shadow-sm or .shadow-lg.

quiz.question: Which class centre-aligns text?
quiz.explanation: text-center sets text-align to centre; text-start and text-end align left/right.

cards.title: Display Utilities
cards.body: d-block makes an element block-level, d-inline makes it inline, d-none hides an element and d-flex creates a flex container. Display classes accept breakpoints: d-none d-md-block hides an element on phones and shows it from md upward.

cards.title: Flexbox Utilities
cards.body: On a .d-flex container, use flex-row / flex-column for direction, justify-content-start | center | end | between | around for main-axis alignment and align-items-start | center | end for cross-axis alignment. Example: <div class="d-flex justify-content-between align-items-center">.

cards.title: Position & Visibility
cards.body: Use position-relative, position-absolute, position-fixed and position-sticky for positioning, and .visible / .invisible to toggle visibility while keeping the space. Use .overflow-auto or .overflow-hidden to control overflow.

quiz.question: Which class turns an element into a flex container?
quiz.explanation: d-flex applies display: flex, enabling the flex utilities such as justify-content-* and align-items-*.

modules.title: Customization with CSS
modules.description: Changing Bootstrap's look with your own styles and following good practice.

cards.title: Overriding Bootstrap Styles
cards.body: Bootstrap provides predefined styles, but they can be changed using custom CSS. Custom CSS can modify colours, fonts, spacing, sizes and the appearance of components.

cards.title: Stylesheet Order Matters
cards.body: A custom stylesheet should be loaded after the Bootstrap CSS so its rules can override Bootstrap styles: <link href="bootstrap.min.css" rel="stylesheet"> followed by <link href="style.css" rel="stylesheet">. When two rules have equal specificity, the one that comes later wins.

cards.title: Combining Bootstrap & Custom Classes
cards.body: Bootstrap classes can be combined with custom classes: <button class="btn btn-primary my-btn">Buy</button>, then in style.css: .my-btn { border-radius: 30px; background-color: #6f42c1; }. Never edit Bootstrap's own files directly; your changes would be lost when you update.

cards.title: Specificity & !important
cards.body: If your rule is not applied, make the selector more specific (e.g. .navbar .my-link) or check the load order. Use !important only as a last resort, as it makes CSS harder to maintain.

quiz.question: Why should custom CSS be loaded after the Bootstrap CSS?
options: So its rules can override Bootstrap's styles
Because Bootstrap requires it to run
So the page uses less memory
quiz.explanation: With equal specificity, the later rule wins, so a stylesheet loaded after Bootstrap can override Bootstrap's defaults.

cards.title: Bootstrap CSS Variables
cards.body: Bootstrap 5 exposes CSS variables such as --bs-primary, --bs-body-bg and --bs-body-font-family. Override them in your own CSS, e.g. :root { --bs-primary: #6f42c1; }, and components can also be tuned locally with variables like --bs-btn-bg.

cards.title: Dark Mode (Bootstrap 5.3)
cards.body: Bootstrap 5.3 supports colour modes through an attribute on the page: <html data-bs-theme="dark">. It switches many components to dark colours without any extra CSS.

cards.title: Customizing with Sass (Overview)
cards.body: For deeper customization, Bootstrap's Sass source lets you change variables like $primary before compiling your own CSS file. This is an advanced option; for most projects, a custom stylesheet loaded after Bootstrap is enough.

cards.title: Best Practices
cards.body: Use utilities and components before writing custom CSS, keep custom CSS in a separate file, use the browser DevTools (Inspect) to see which rules apply and why, test on real screen sizes, and avoid overusing !important.

quiz.question: Which attribute enables Bootstrap 5.3's dark mode?
quiz.explanation: Setting data-bs-theme="dark" on <html> (or a container) switches Bootstrap 5.3 components to the dark colour mode.

units.title: Module 5: JavaScript
units.description: Make web pages interactive: from core language fundamentals to the DOM, events, forms, storage and modern ES6+ JavaScript.

modules.title: JavaScript Basics
modules.description: Meet JavaScript, add it to a page, and master variables, data types and operators.

cards.title: What is JavaScript?
cards.body: JavaScript is the interpreted, object-oriented-capable language that makes web pages dynamic. HTML gives structure, CSS gives style, JavaScript gives behavior. Created in 1995 by Brendan Eich at Netscape (Mocha, LiveScript, JavaScript) and standardized as ECMAScript. It is unrelated to Java.

cards.title: Client-Side vs Server-Side
cards.body: Client-side scripts run in the user's browser; server-side code (Python, PHP, Node.js) runs on the server. Client-side JS is fast, validates input instantly and is easy to learn, but it is less secure, has no hardware access and needs a JS-enabled browser.

cards.title: Adding JavaScript to HTML
cards.body: Add JavaScript three ways: inline (onclick attribute), internal (<script> in head or end of body) and external (<script src='app.js'>). External files are best practice: cleaner HTML, browser caching and reuse. Place scripts at the end of body or use defer.

cards.title: Displaying Output & Comments
cards.body: Use console.log() to debug, alert() for dialogs, and innerHTML or textContent to write into the page. document.write() erases the whole page if called after loading, so use it only for testing. Comments: // for one line, /* ... */ for many.

quiz.question: Which is the recommended way to include a large amount of JavaScript in a web page?
options: An external .js file linked with <script src="...">
quiz.explanation: External files keep HTML clean, can be cached by the browser, and are reusable across many pages.

cards.title: Identifiers & Variable Rules
cards.body: A variable is a named container for a value. Names may use letters, digits, _ and $, cannot start with a digit, cannot contain spaces or reserved keywords, and are case-sensitive. JavaScript is dynamically typed, and a declared variable without a value is undefined.

cards.title: var, let and const
cards.body: var is function-scoped, re-declarable and hoisted. let is block-scoped and reassignable. const is block-scoped, must be initialised and cannot be reassigned, though object contents can change. Best practice: use const by default, let when the value changes, and avoid var.

cards.title: Primitive & Non-Primitive Types
cards.body: Primitive types: String, Number, Boolean, Undefined, Null (plus Symbol, BigInt). Non-primitive types: Object, Array, Date, RegExp, Function. The typeof operator returns the type as a string, e.g. typeof 'a' is 'string'. Quirk: typeof null returns 'object'.

cards.title: Undefined vs Null, Scope & Hoisting
cards.body: undefined means no value was assigned; null means deliberately empty. Global variables are visible everywhere, local ones only inside their function, and let/const also have block scope. Hoisting moves declarations (not values) to the top, so a var read early gives undefined.

quiz.question: What is the output of: let a; console.log(typeof a);
quiz.explanation: A variable declared without a value holds undefined, and typeof undefined returns the string 'undefined'.

cards.title: Arithmetic & Assignment Operators
cards.body: Arithmetic operators: + - * / % ** plus ++ and --. Assignment: = += -= *= /=. The + operator also concatenates strings: '5' + 3 gives '53', but '5' - 3 gives 2. Dividing by zero gives Infinity; invalid math gives NaN.

cards.title: Comparison Operators
cards.body: Comparison operators: > < >= <= == != === !==. The == operator converts types (5 == '5' is true), while === checks value and type (5 === '5' is false). Always prefer === and !==. NaN never equals anything, so test it with Number.isNaN().

cards.title: Logical & Bitwise Operators
cards.body: Logical operators: && (AND), || (OR), ! (NOT). They short-circuit and return the deciding operand. Falsy values are false, 0, '', null, undefined and NaN. Bitwise operators work on binary bits: & (AND), | (OR), ^ (XOR), ~ (NOT) and the shifts << and >>.

cards.title: Ternary, typeof & User Input
cards.body: The ternary operator is a compact if-else: condition ? valueIfTrue : valueIfFalse. To read input, prompt('Enter name:') shows a dialog and always returns a string (or null if cancelled). Convert it with Number(), parseInt() or parseFloat() before doing math.

quiz.question: What does ('5' + 3) evaluate to in JavaScript?
quiz.explanation: When one operand of + is a string, JavaScript converts the other to a string and concatenates: '5' + 3 = '53'.

modules.title: Control Flow
modules.description: Make decisions and repeat actions with conditional statements and loops.

cards.title: if, if-else and else-if
cards.body: if (condition) { ... } runs a block only when the condition is truthy. Add else for the alternative and chain else if for multi-way decisions. Combine conditions with && and ||. Braces are optional for single statements but strongly recommended for readability.

cards.title: switch Statement
cards.body: switch compares an expression against case values using strict equality (===). Without break, execution falls through into the next case. Stack cases to share one block, and default runs when nothing matches. Use switch for fixed values and if-else for ranges.

cards.title: Ternary & Truthy/Falsy Checks
cards.body: For simple choices use the ternary: const status = age >= 18 ? 'Adult' : 'Minor'. In conditions, falsy values are false, 0, '', null, undefined and NaN; everything else, including '0', [] and {}, is truthy. So if (name) checks that a string is not empty.

quiz.question: What happens in a switch statement if you forget the 'break' after a matching case?
options: Execution continues into the following cases (fall-through)
The default case is skipped and nothing runs
quiz.explanation: Without break, JavaScript keeps executing the statements of the next cases until it hits a break or the end of the switch.

cards.title: for Loop & Nested Loops
cards.body: for (init; condition; update) suits a known number of iterations: for (let i = 0; i < 5; i++). Each part is optional. A loop inside another loop is nested: the inner loop runs fully for every outer iteration, which is how patterns and tables are built.

cards.title: while and do-while
cards.body: while checks its condition before each iteration, so it may run zero times. do...while checks after the body, so it always runs at least once, which suits menus and input retries. Always update the loop variable, or you create an infinite loop.

cards.title: for-in and for-of
cards.body: for...in iterates over an object's keys (property names). for...of iterates over the values of iterables such as arrays and strings. Avoid for...in on arrays because it returns indexes as strings. Arrays also offer the forEach() method for iteration.

cards.title: break, continue & Labels
cards.body: break exits a loop completely; continue skips the current iteration and moves to the next. In a loop from 1 to 10, continue at 3 skips only 3, while break at 3 stops after 2. Labels let break leave nested loops.

quiz.question: Which loop is guaranteed to execute its body at least once?
quiz.explanation: do...while checks its condition after running the body, so the body always runs once before the first check.

modules.title: Functions & Data Structures
modules.description: Write reusable functions and work with arrays, strings, numbers, Math and dates.

cards.title: Declaring & Calling Functions
cards.body: A function is a reusable block of code. Declare it with function greet(name) { return 'Hello ' + name; } and call greet('Asha'). The code runs only when called. Function declarations are hoisted, so they can be called before they appear in the file.

cards.title: Parameters, Defaults & Rest
cards.body: JavaScript does not check argument types or counts: missing arguments become undefined and extras are ignored. Default parameters provide fallbacks: function add(a, b = 10). Rest parameters collect extra arguments into a real array: function sum(...nums). The rest parameter must come last.

cards.title: return, Scope & Closures
cards.body: return sends a value back and stops the function; without it the result is undefined. Inner functions can read outer variables, not vice versa. A closure is an inner function that remembers its outer variables even after the outer function finishes, useful for private counters.

cards.title: Pass by Value vs Reference
cards.body: Primitives (numbers, strings, booleans) are passed by value, so changes inside a function do not affect the original. Objects and arrays are passed as references, so changing their properties inside a function is visible outside. Reassigning the parameter itself does not affect the caller.

quiz.question: A function is called as add(10, 20) but is defined as function add(a, b, c). What is c inside the function?
quiz.explanation: Missing arguments are set to undefined; JavaScript does not throw an error for fewer arguments.

cards.title: Function Expressions & Anonymous Functions
cards.body: A function can be stored in a variable: const show = function() {...}. Function expressions are not hoisted, so calling them early fails. Anonymous functions have no name and can be stored, passed as callbacks or returned from other functions.

cards.title: Arrow Functions
cards.body: Arrow functions have shorter syntax: const add = (a, b) => a + b. One parameter needs no parentheses; zero parameters use (). A single expression is returned implicitly, but with braces you need return. Arrow functions are anonymous and inherit this from surrounding code.

cards.title: IIFE & Callbacks
cards.body: An IIFE runs immediately after definition: (function() { ... })(). It creates a private scope and avoids polluting global variables. A callback is a function passed to another function to run later, such as setTimeout(() => console.log('Done'), 1000) or arr.forEach(fn).

quiz.question: Which arrow function correctly returns the sum of a and b?
quiz.explanation: With a single expression and no braces, an arrow function returns the value implicitly. With braces you must write return.

cards.title: Creating & Accessing Arrays
cards.body: Arrays store multiple values under one name and are zero-indexed: const fruits = ['Apple', 'Mango']. Use fruits[0] to access, length for the count, and an invalid index returns undefined. Arrays are objects, so check with Array.isArray(). Nested arrays create 2D structures.

cards.title: Adding, Removing & Copying
cards.body: push() and pop() add or remove at the end; unshift() and shift() work at the start. splice(start, count, ...items) edits anywhere and changes the original. slice(start, end) copies a portion without changing it. Also useful: concat(), join(), reverse(), indexOf(), includes(), fill().

cards.title: Iterating & Transforming
cards.body: Loop with for, for...of or forEach(). map() returns a new transformed array, filter() keeps items passing a test, and reduce() combines everything into one value. find() returns the first match. sort() sorts as strings by default, so pass a compare function for numbers.

quiz.question: Which array method returns a NEW array containing the result of calling a function on every element?
quiz.explanation: map() builds and returns a new array of transformed values and leaves the original untouched; forEach returns nothing.

cards.title: String Methods & Template Literals
cards.body: Strings accept single, double or backtick quotes. Template literals support multi-line text and interpolation: `Hello ${name}`. Common methods: slice(), indexOf(), toUpperCase(), trim(), replace(), split(), includes(). Strings are immutable, so methods return new strings.

cards.title: Numbers, NaN & Conversion
cards.body: All numbers are 64-bit floating point, so 0.1 + 0.2 is not exactly 0.3. Special values are NaN and Infinity. Convert with Number(), parseInt('15.45') gives 15 and parseFloat('15.45') gives 15.45. Format with toFixed(2); check with Number.isNaN() and Number.isInteger().

cards.title: The Math Object
cards.body: Math is a built-in static object. It has constants Math.PI and Math.E, and methods round(), ceil(), floor(), abs(), pow(), sqrt(), max(), min() and random() (0 up to, not including, 1). Random integer from 1 to 10: Math.floor(Math.random() * 10) + 1.

cards.title: Working with Dates
cards.body: Create dates with new Date() (now), new Date(year, month, day) or an ISO string. Months and weekdays start at 0 (January = 0, Sunday = 0), but days of the month start at 1. Use getFullYear(), getMonth(), getDate(), setDate() and toLocaleDateString().

quiz.question: What does new Date(2025, 0, 15) represent?
quiz.explanation: JavaScript months are zero-based, so 0 means January while the day of the month starts at 1.

modules.title: JavaScript Objects & OOP
modules.description: Model real-world things with objects, constructors, prototypes and ES6 classes.

cards.title: Creating Objects
cards.body: An object holds key-value pairs called properties; a property holding a function is a method. The literal form is preferred: const student = { name: 'Rahul', age: 20, greet() { return 'Hi ' + this.name; } }. Keys with spaces need quotes.

cards.title: Accessing, Adding & Deleting
cards.body: Read properties with dot notation (student.name) or brackets (student['name']); brackets are needed for spaced or dynamic keys. Add or update with student.city = 'Delhi' and remove with delete student.age. Inside a method, this refers to the calling object.

cards.title: Checking Properties & Looping
cards.body: Check for a key with the in operator ('name' in student) or hasOwnProperty('name'). Loop with for...in or use Object.keys(), Object.values() and Object.entries(). Copy or merge objects with spread: { ...a, ...b }. Object.freeze() blocks further changes.

cards.title: JSON & Built-in Objects
cards.body: JSON is a text format for data exchange: JSON.stringify(obj) converts an object to a string and JSON.parse(str) converts it back. JavaScript objects include user-defined, native (Array, Date, Math), host (window, navigator) and DOM objects such as document.

quiz.question: How do you correctly access a property whose key is stored in a variable named key?
quiz.explanation: Bracket notation evaluates the variable and uses its value as the property name; obj.key would look for a property literally named 'key'.

cards.title: Factory & Constructor Functions
cards.body: A factory function simply returns a new object. A constructor function is called with new and sets properties using this: function Mobile(model) { this.model = model; }. Constructor names conventionally start with a capital letter. Forgetting new is a common bug.

cards.title: Prototypes & the Prototype Chain
cards.body: Every object inherits from a prototype. Property lookup climbs the prototype chain: object, Constructor.prototype, Object.prototype, then null. Methods placed on Mobile.prototype are shared by all instances, saving memory. Object.create(proto) makes an object with a chosen prototype.

cards.title: ES6 Classes
cards.body: ES6 classes are cleaner syntax over prototypes: class Mobile { constructor(model) { this.model = model; } show() {...} }. A class has one constructor and is not hoisted. static methods belong to the class itself, and private fields use #price.

cards.title: Inheritance, super & Overriding
cards.body: extends creates a child class: class Smart extends Mobile. In a child constructor, call super() before using this. A child can override a parent method and still call it with super.show(). OOP's pillars: encapsulation, abstraction, inheritance and polymorphism.

quiz.question: In a child class constructor, what must you do before using 'this'?
quiz.explanation: A derived class must call super() first, which initialises the parent part of the object and makes 'this' available.

modules.title: DOM, Events & Forms
modules.description: Control the page with the DOM, respond to user actions, use popups and validate forms.

cards.title: What is the DOM?
cards.body: The Document Object Model (DOM) is the browser's tree representation of an HTML page; every tag becomes a node JavaScript can read and change. The document object is the entry point. Changing the DOM updates the page instantly without reloading.

cards.title: Selecting Elements
cards.body: getElementById('id') returns one element. The flexible modern methods are querySelector('.card > h2') for the first match and querySelectorAll('li.item') for all matches. Run scripts after the HTML loads: end of body, defer, or the DOMContentLoaded event.

cards.title: Changing Content, Attributes & Styles
cards.body: Change content with textContent (plain text, safe) or innerHTML (parses HTML, risky with user input). Set attributes with setAttribute(). Set styles with el.style.color = 'red'. Prefer toggling CSS classes using classList.add(), remove(), toggle() and contains().

cards.title: Creating, Inserting & Removing Elements
cards.body: Create nodes with document.createElement('li'), set textContent, then insert with appendChild(), append(), prepend() or insertAdjacentHTML(). Delete with el.remove(). Navigate the tree using parentElement, children, nextElementSibling and previousElementSibling.

quiz.question: Which property is the safest way to put plain text coming from a user into an element?
quiz.explanation: textContent inserts text without parsing it as HTML, preventing injected scripts (XSS) that innerHTML can allow.

cards.title: Event Handling Basics
cards.body: Events are user or browser actions: click, input, change, submit, keydown, focus, load. Attach handlers with addEventListener('click', fn); it allows many handlers per event and can be removed with removeEventListener. It is preferred over inline onclick attributes.

cards.title: The Event Object, Bubbling & Delegation
cards.body: The handler receives an event object: e.target is the clicked element, e.key gives the keyboard key, and e.preventDefault() stops default behavior like form submit. Events bubble up to ancestors, so one parent listener can handle all children (event delegation).

cards.title: Popup Boxes: alert, confirm, prompt
cards.body: Three built-in popup boxes: alert('msg') shows a message; confirm('Sure?') shows OK/Cancel and returns true or false; prompt('Name?') shows a text field and returns the string, or null if cancelled. They block the page, so use sparingly.

cards.title: Timers
cards.body: setTimeout(fn, ms) runs a function once after a delay; setInterval(fn, ms) repeats it. Stop them with clearTimeout(id) and clearInterval(id). Timers are asynchronous: the rest of your code keeps running while waiting for them.

quiz.question: What does confirm('Are you sure?') return when the user clicks Cancel?
quiz.explanation: confirm() returns true for OK and false for Cancel; prompt() is the one that returns null on cancel.

cards.title: Accessing Form Data
cards.body: Select a form with getElementById or document.forms, and read fields using input.value or input.checked for checkboxes. Listen with form.addEventListener('submit', fn) and call e.preventDefault() to stop the reload. Remember input.value is always a string.

cards.title: Basic Validation Techniques
cards.body: Typical checks: required fields (value.trim() !== ''), minimum length, numeric range (Number(age) >= 18), matching passwords and email format. Show an error message beside the field, highlight it with a CSS class, and call e.preventDefault() when any check fails.

cards.title: Regular Expressions for Validation
cards.body: A regex tests text patterns: /^\d{10}$/.test(value) validates a 10-digit phone number, and /^[A-Za-z ]+$/ allows letters only. test() returns true or false. HTML5 attributes (required, minlength, pattern, type='email') provide built-in validation too.

cards.title: Validation Best Practices
cards.body: Validate on the client for fast feedback and on the server for security; users can bypass JavaScript. Validate on the input event or on blur, give clear messages like 'Password must be at least 8 characters', and avoid alert() popups for every error.

quiz.question: Why must a form still be validated on the server even if JavaScript validation exists?
options: Users can disable or bypass client-side JavaScript
HTML forms don't work without it
quiz.explanation: Client-side validation is for convenience; attackers or users can disable or alter JavaScript, so the server must verify all data.

modules.title: Robust & Modern JavaScript
modules.description: Handle errors, organise code in modules, store data in the browser and use ES6+ features.

cards.title: Types of Errors & try...catch
cards.body: Common errors: SyntaxError (invalid code), ReferenceError (undeclared variable), TypeError (wrong type) and RangeError. Wrap risky code in try { } catch (err) { console.error(err.message); } so scripts don't crash. The optional finally block always runs, ideal for cleanup.

cards.title: throw & Custom Errors
cards.body: Raise your own error with throw new Error('Age cannot be negative'). Create custom types with class ValidationError extends Error {}. In async code use try/catch with await or .catch() on promises. Debug using console.log, console.table, DevTools breakpoints and the debugger statement.

quiz.question: When does the finally block of a try...catch...finally statement execute?
options: Always, whether or not an error occurred
quiz.explanation: finally runs in every case - after try succeeds or after catch handles the error - making it ideal for cleanup code.

cards.title: export and import
cards.body: ES modules split code into reusable files. Export with export function add() {} (named) or export default (one per file). Import with import { add } from './math.js' or import calc from './math.js'. Use import * as math and 'as' to rename.

cards.title: Using Modules in the Browser
cards.body: Load a module with <script type='module' src='main.js'>. Modules run in strict mode, have their own scope, run once, and are deferred automatically. They must be served over http(s), not file://. Benefits: maintainability, reuse and no global name clashes.

quiz.question: How do you load a JavaScript ES module in an HTML page?
quiz.explanation: The type="module" attribute tells the browser to treat the file as an ES module with import/export support.

cards.title: Web Storage Basics
cards.body: The Web Storage API saves key-value strings in the browser, about 5 MB per origin. localStorage persists after the browser closes; sessionStorage lasts only for the current tab. Methods: setItem(), getItem() (null if missing), removeItem(), clear() and the length property.

cards.title: Storing Objects & Use Cases
cards.body: Values must be strings, so convert objects with JSON: localStorage.setItem('user', JSON.stringify(user)) and JSON.parse(localStorage.getItem('user')). Common uses: theme, cart, to-do lists, form drafts. Never store passwords or sensitive tokens there; any page script can read them.

quiz.question: Which statement about sessionStorage is correct?
options: Data persists forever until manually cleared
Data is shared across all browser tabs
Data is cleared when the tab/session is closed
It can store objects directly without conversion
quiz.explanation: sessionStorage is scoped to a single tab and ends when that tab or window is closed; localStorage is the persistent one.

cards.title: Destructuring, Spread & Rest
cards.body: Destructuring unpacks values: const [a, b] = [1, 2]; const { name, age = 18 } = student. The spread operator expands iterables: [...arr1, ...arr2] and { ...obj, city: 'Delhi' }. The same ... syntax collects function arguments as rest parameters.

cards.title: Template Literals, Optional Chaining & More
cards.body: Template literals: `Total: ${price * qty}`. Optional chaining user?.address?.city returns undefined instead of throwing. Nullish coalescing count ?? 0 falls back only for null or undefined, unlike || which also replaces 0 and ''. Shorthand properties { name, age } are also ES6+.

cards.title: Promises, async/await & fetch
cards.body: A Promise represents a future value (pending, fulfilled, rejected), used with .then() and .catch(). async/await makes asynchronous code read like normal code: const res = await fetch(url); const data = await res.json(). Wrap in try/catch and check res.ok.

cards.title: Other Useful Modern Features
cards.body: Useful modern features: array methods (map, filter, reduce, find, some, every, flat), Object.entries(), Set and Map collections, BigInt for huge integers, and classes with private fields. New ECMAScript editions keep adding features, so keep learning from MDN Web Docs.

quiz.question: What does user?.address?.city return if user.address is undefined?
quiz.explanation: Optional chaining (?.) short-circuits and returns undefined instead of throwing an error when part of the path is null or undefined.

units.title: Module 6: Python Basics
units.description: Python from first program to functions, files and modules: the complete core-language foundation for backend development.

modules.title: Introduction to Python & Setup
modules.description: What Python is, how your code actually runs, how to install it, and the core building blocks: variables, keywords, indentation and I/O.

cards.title: What is Python?
cards.body: Python is a high-level, interpreted, dynamically typed, object-oriented programming language known for clean, readable syntax. It blends ideas from C and Java but needs far less code to do the same job. It is used for web backends (Django, Flask), data science and ML (NumPy, scikit-learn, TensorFlow), automation, desktop GUIs (Tkinter), games and scripting.

cards.title: History & Versions
cards.body: Guido van Rossum began Python in the late 1980s at CWI in the Netherlands as a successor to the ABC language; the name comes from the TV show 'Monty Python's Flying Circus'. Key releases: 0.9.0 (Feb 1991), 1.0 (Jan 1994), 2.0 (Oct 2000), 3.0 (Dec 2008). Python 2 was officially retired on 1 Jan 2020, so all new work uses Python 3.

cards.title: Key Features
cards.body: Easy to learn and read, interpreted (no separate compile-and-link step), platform independent (same code runs on Windows, Linux, macOS), supports both procedural and object-oriented styles, has a huge standard library plus 400k+ third-party packages on PyPI, and scales from 5-line scripts to large production systems.

quiz.question: Who created the Python programming language?
quiz.explanation: Python was created by Guido van Rossum. Gosling made Java, Ritchie made C, and Stroustrup made C++.

cards.title: Bytecode & the PVM
cards.body: When you run a program, CPython first compiles the source (.py) into bytecode, a compact set of low-level instructions (cached as .pyc files inside __pycache__). The Python Virtual Machine (PVM) then interprets that bytecode one instruction at a time and asks the CPU to execute it. The compile step is automatic and invisible: you never run a separate compiler.

cards.title: Python Implementations
cards.body: 'Python' is a language; interpreters implement it. CPython (written in C) is the standard one you get from python.org. Others include Jython (runs on the JVM), IronPython (.NET), and PyPy (a faster interpreter with a just-in-time compiler). Anaconda is not a different interpreter; it is a distribution that bundles CPython with many packages.

cards.title: Ways to Run Python Code
cards.body: Interactive mode (REPL): type 'python' and run one statement at a time, ideal for experiments. Script mode: save code in 'hello.py' and run 'python hello.py'. You can also use IDLE, Jupyter notebooks, or an IDE such as VS Code or PyCharm, which add editing, debugging and run buttons on top of the same interpreter.

quiz.question: Which component executes Python bytecode?
quiz.explanation: Source code is compiled to bytecode, and the PVM interprets that bytecode and drives the machine instructions.

cards.title: Installing Python on Windows
cards.body: Download the latest Python 3 installer from python.org, run it, and tick 'Add python.exe to PATH' on the first screen before clicking Install Now; this avoids the 'python is not recognized' error. Verify in Command Prompt with 'python --version' (or 'py --version') and 'pip --version'. pip is installed automatically.

cards.title: Installing Python on Linux
cards.body: Most Linux distributions ship Python 3 already; check with 'python3 --version'. On Debian/Ubuntu install or update it with 'sudo apt install python3 python3-pip python3-venv'; on Fedora use 'sudo dnf install python3'. Run scripts with 'python3 file.py'. Avoid replacing the system Python; create isolated environments with 'python3 -m venv myenv' instead.

cards.title: Python IDEs & Editors
cards.body: IDLE ships with Python and is fine for beginners. VS Code (with the Python extension) is a light, popular editor; PyCharm is a full-featured IDE with refactoring and debugging; Spyder is aimed at scientific work; Jupyter Notebook mixes code, output and notes in one document. All of them use the same underlying Python interpreter.

cards.title: Introduction to Anaconda (Part 1)
cards.body: Anaconda is a distribution for data science and ML that bundles Python, the 'conda' package/environment manager, and hundreds of pre-installed libraries (NumPy, pandas, Matplotlib), plus tools like Jupyter and Spyder via Anaconda Navigator.

cards.title: Introduction to Anaconda (Part 2)
cards.body: Useful commands: 'conda create -n myenv python=3.12', 'conda activate myenv', 'conda install numpy'. Miniconda is the lightweight version with only conda and Python.

quiz.question: During Windows installation, which option prevents the 'python is not recognized' error?
quiz.explanation: Adding Python to PATH lets the command prompt find the 'python' command from any folder.

cards.title: Variables & Identifiers (Part 1)
cards.body: A variable is a name (tag) bound to an object; no type declaration is needed ('age = 25'). Identifier rules: start with a letter or underscore, contain only letters, digits and underscores, no spaces, no keywords, and names are case-sensitive ('rahul' is not 'Rahul').

cards.title: Variables & Identifiers (Part 2)
cards.body: Convention: snake_case for variables, UPPER_CASE for constants (Python does not enforce constants). Multiple assignment: 'a, b = 1, 2'; swap with 'a, b = b, a'.

cards.title: How Python Handles Variables
cards.body: Because variables are tags on objects, 'a = 10; b = 10' makes both names point to the same int object, and 'a = 20' simply moves the tag 'a' to a new object. When an object has no names pointing to it, the garbage collector frees its memory. 'id(a)' shows the object's identity and 'type(a)' its type; Python is dynamically typed, so the same name can later refer to a string.

cards.title: Keywords (Part 1)
cards.body: Keywords are reserved words with special meaning and cannot be used as identifiers. Python 3 has 35, such as: False None True and as assert async await break class continue def del elif else except finally for from global if import in is lambda nonlocal not or pass raise return try while with yield.

cards.title: Keywords (Part 2)
cards.body: List them with 'import keyword; print(keyword.kwlist)'. Keywords are case-sensitive: 'True' is a keyword, 'true' is not.

cards.title: Indentation & Comments
cards.body: Python uses indentation (conventionally 4 spaces) instead of braces to mark blocks; a block begins after a colon, e.g. 'if x > 0:'. All lines in a block must be indented equally, otherwise Python raises IndentationError. Comments start with '#'; there is no true multi-line comment, but triple-quoted strings are often used as docstrings to document functions and classes.

quiz.question: What happens if statements inside the same block have inconsistent indentation?
quiz.explanation: Indentation defines blocks in Python, so inconsistent indentation causes an IndentationError (or a wrong program structure).

cards.title: Output with print()
cards.body: 'print(*objects, sep=' ', end='\n', file=sys.stdout, flush=False)' displays values. 'sep' controls the separator ('print(1, 2, 3, sep="-")' gives 1-2-3) and 'end' controls what is printed at the end ('end=""' stays on the same line). Escape sequences: \n newline, \t tab, \ backslash, \' and " quotes. For readable output use f-strings: 'print(f"Name: {name}, Age: {age}")'.

cards.title: Input with input()
cards.body: 'input(prompt)' pauses the program, shows the prompt, and returns whatever the user types as a string, even if they type digits. Convert explicitly: 'age = int(input("Age: "))', 'price = float(input())'. Read several numbers on one line with 'a, b = map(int, input().split())'. Entering text where a number is expected raises ValueError.

cards.title: Type Conversion
cards.body: Implicit conversion: Python converts automatically when safe, e.g. 'int + float' gives float ('5 / 2' is 2.5). Explicit conversion (casting) is done with int(), float(), str(), list(), tuple(), set(), bool(), bin(), oct(), hex(), complex(). Note 'int(3.9)' truncates to 3 and 'int("abc")' raises ValueError.

quiz.question: What is the data type of the value returned by input()?
options: It depends on what the user types
quiz.explanation: input() always returns a string. Use int() or float() to convert it to a number.

modules.title: Python Operators
modules.description: Every operator category in Python: arithmetic, comparison, assignment, logical, bitwise, membership, identity, ternary, and precedence.

cards.title: Arithmetic Operators
cards.body: '+' add, '-' subtract, '*' multiply, '/' true division (always returns float: 7 / 2 = 3.5), '//' floor division (7 // 2 = 3, but -7 // 2 = -4 because it rounds down), '%' modulus (7 % 3 = 1; -7 % 3 = 2, the result takes the divisor's sign), '**' power (2 ** 3 = 8). '+' and '*' also work on strings and lists: 'ab' * 3 gives 'ababab'.

cards.title: Comparison (Relational) Operators
cards.body: '==', '!=', '<', '>', '<=', '>=' compare two values and return True or False. Python allows chained comparisons: '1 < x < 10' means '1 < x and x < 10'. Strings compare alphabetically by character code ('A' < 'B' is True). Beware of floats: '0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3' is False because of binary rounding; use 'math.isclose()' instead.

cards.title: Assignment Operators
cards.body: '=' assigns a value; compound operators combine an operation with assignment: '+=', '-=', '*=', '/=', '//=', '%=', '**=', and the bitwise forms '&=', '|=', '^=', '<<=', '>>='. 'x += 5' is shorthand for 'x = x + 5'. Python 3.8 added the walrus operator ':=' which assigns inside an expression, e.g. 'if (n := len(data)) > 10:'.

quiz.question: What is the value of -7 // 2 in Python?
quiz.explanation: Floor division rounds toward negative infinity, so -3.5 becomes -4.

cards.title: Logical Operators
cards.body: 'and', 'or', 'not' combine conditions. They short-circuit: 'and' stops at the first falsy operand, 'or' stops at the first truthy one, and they return the operand itself, not strictly True/False ('0 or "hi"' gives 'hi'; '"a" and "b"' gives 'b'). Falsy values: 0, 0.0, '', [], (), {}, set(), None and False; everything else is truthy.

cards.title: Bitwise Operators
cards.body: Bitwise operators work on the binary digits of integers: '&' AND, '|' OR, '^' XOR, '~' NOT, '<<' left shift, '>>' right shift. With a = 10 (1010) and b = 15 (1111): 'a & b' = 10, 'a | b' = 15, 'a ^ b' = 5, '~a' = -11, 'a << 2' = 40 (multiply by 4), 'a >> 2' = 2 (divide by 4). Used for flags, masks and low-level optimisation.

cards.title: Membership Operators
cards.body: 'in' and 'not in' test whether a value exists in a sequence or collection. For strings they check substrings ('"to" in "Welcome to Python"' is True); for lists, tuples and sets they check elements; for dictionaries they check keys ('101 in stu'). Membership tests on sets and dicts are very fast compared with lists.

cards.title: Identity Operators
cards.body: 'is' and 'is not' check whether two names refer to the exact same object in memory (same id()), whereas '==' checks whether values are equal. '[1] == [1]' is True but '[1] is [1]' is False. Small integers and some strings are cached by CPython so 'a = 10; b = 10; a is b' is True, but never rely on this. Use 'is' only for None checks: 'if x is None'.

quiz.question: What is the result of 10 ^ 15 in Python?
quiz.explanation: XOR gives 1 only where bits differ: 1010 ^ 1111 = 0101, which is 5.

cards.title: Ternary (Conditional) Operator
cards.body: Python's one-line conditional expression is 'value_if_true if condition else value_if_false'. Example: 'status = "Pass" if marks >= 40 else "Fail"'. It can be nested ('"A" if m > 90 else "B" if m > 75 else "C"') but readability drops quickly, so switch to if-elif-else for more than two outcomes.

cards.title: Operator Precedence & Associativity (Part 1)
cards.body: When an expression has several operators, precedence decides the order. From highest to lowest: parentheses (), '**', unary +x -x ~x, '* / // %', '+ -', '<< >>', '&', '^', '|', comparisons (including in, not in, is, is not), 'not', 'and', 'or', ternary if-else, lambda, assignment.

cards.title: Operator Precedence & Associativity (Part 2)
cards.body: Operators of equal precedence evaluate left to right, except '**' which is right to left: '2 ** 3 ** 2' = 2 ** 9 = 512.

cards.title: Worked Example
cards.body: Evaluate '(1+1)*2**4//3+4-1': parentheses first gives '2*2**4//3+4-1'; then '**' gives '2*16//3+4-1'; then '*' and '//' left to right give '32//3' = 10, so '10+4-1'; finally left to right gives 13. When in doubt, add parentheses to make the order obvious.

quiz.question: What is the value of 2 ** 3 ** 2?
quiz.explanation: The ** operator is right-associative: 3 ** 2 = 9 first, then 2 ** 9 = 512.

modules.title: Python's Built-in Data Types
modules.description: Numbers, None, strings, lists, tuples, sets, dictionaries, arrays (array module and NumPy) and regular expressions, with their characteristics and methods.

cards.title: Numeric Types
cards.body: int: whole numbers with unlimited size ('2 ** 200' works). float: decimal numbers stored as 64-bit doubles, also scientific notation ('5.1e5' = 510000.0). complex: 'a + bj' such as '5 + 7j' with '.real' and '.imag'. Other int bases: 0b1010 (binary), 0o12 (octal), 0xA (hex); underscores improve readability ('1_000_000'). Useful: abs(), round(), pow(), divmod().

cards.title: bool and None
cards.body: bool has two values, True and False, and is a subclass of int, so 'True + True' = 2 and 'True - False' = 1. None is the single value of type NoneType and means 'no value'; a function without a return statement returns None. Compare with 'is None', not '== None'. Python has no separate char type: a single character is just a string of length 1.

quiz.question: Which statement about None is correct?
options: None is the same as an empty string
None represents the absence of a value and is falsy
None is a keyword for loops
quiz.explanation: None is a special NoneType object meaning 'no value'. It is falsy but not equal to 0 or ''.

cards.title: Creating Strings
cards.body: Strings are sequences of characters in single, double or triple quotes (triple quotes allow multiple lines). Mix quote types to include quotes ('He said "hi"') or use escapes ('\n', '\t'). A raw string 'r"C:\new\folder"' disables escapes, handy for Windows paths and regex. 'len(s)' gives the length.

cards.title: Indexing & Immutability
cards.body: Characters are accessed by index starting at 0; negative indexes count from the end ('s[-1]' is the last character). Strings are immutable: 's[0] = "X"' raises TypeError, so every 'modification' (replace, upper, etc.) returns a new string. Iterate with 'for ch in s:' or 'for i in range(len(s))'.

cards.title: Slicing & String Operators
cards.body: 's[start:stop:step]' returns a piece of the string: start is included, stop is excluded, and defaults are 0, len and 1. Examples with s = 'Python': 's[1:4]' = 'yth', 's[:2]' = 'Py', 's[::-1]' = 'nohtyP'. Operators: '+' concatenates, '*' repeats, '==' and '<' compare alphabetically, and 'in' tests for a substring.

quiz.question: What does 'Python'[1:4] return?
quiz.explanation: Slicing starts at index 1 ('y') and stops before index 4, giving 'yth'.

cards.title: Common String Methods
cards.body: Case: upper(), lower(), title(), capitalize(), swapcase(). Tests: isupper(), islower(), isdigit(), isalpha(), isalnum(), isspace(), startswith(), endswith(). Cleaning: strip(), lstrip(), rstrip(). Search: find() (returns -1 if absent), index() (raises ValueError), count(). Transform: replace(old, new), split(sep) returns a list, 'sep'.join(list) builds a string. All return new strings.

cards.title: String Formatting
cards.body: Three styles exist. C-style: '"%s is %d" % (name, age)'. str.format(): '"{} is {}".format(name, age)' or with positions/names '{0}', '{n}'. f-strings (Python 3.6+, recommended): 'f"{name} is {age}"'. Format spec after a colon controls output: 'f"{price:8.2f}"' (width 8, 2 decimals), 'f"{n:05d}"' (zero-padded), 'f"{s:^10}"' (centered), 'f"{n:,}"' (thousand separators).

quiz.question: Which string method splits a string into a list of pieces?
quiz.explanation: split(separator) breaks a string into a list. join() does the opposite: it combines a list into one string.

cards.title: List Characteristics
cards.body: A list is an ordered, mutable, dynamic collection written in square brackets and may hold mixed types: 'data = [10, 20, -50, 21.3, "text"]'. It supports indexing (also negative), slicing, '+' concatenation, '*' repetition, 'in' tests, and nesting ('m[1][0]'). Modify with 'data[1] = 40'; delete with 'del data[2]'. Create from other iterables with 'list("abc")' or 'list(range(5))'.

cards.title: List Methods
cards.body: append(x) adds at the end; insert(i, x) adds at a position; extend(iterable) appends many; remove(x) deletes the first match (ValueError if absent); pop() removes and returns the last item, pop(i) the item at i; index(x), count(x), reverse(), clear(), copy(). 'sort()' sorts in place ('reverse=True', 'key=len' supported), while 'sorted(lst)' returns a new sorted list.

cards.title: Aliasing vs Copying
cards.body: 'b = a' does not copy: both names refer to the same list, so changing one changes the other. For an independent (shallow) copy use 'a.copy()', 'a[:]' or 'list(a)'. A shallow copy still shares nested lists; use 'copy.deepcopy(a)' when the list contains other lists.

cards.title: List Comprehension
cards.body: A compact way to build lists: '[expression for item in iterable if condition]'. Examples: '[i*i for i in range(5)]' gives [0, 1, 4, 9, 16]; '[i for i in range(20) if i % 2 == 0]' gives the even numbers; '[x if x % 2 == 0 else "odd" for x in range(5)]' uses if-else in the expression part. Similar syntax works for sets and dicts.

quiz.question: After 'a = [1, 2, 3]; b = a; a.append(4)', what is b?
quiz.explanation: b = a creates an alias, not a copy, so both names refer to the same list object.

cards.title: Tuples (Part 1)
cards.body: A tuple is an ordered, immutable sequence in parentheses: 't = (10, 20, "x")'. Elements cannot be changed, which makes tuples safe for fixed data, slightly faster and smaller than lists, and usable as dictionary keys (if their contents are immutable).

cards.title: Tuples (Part 2)
cards.body: A single-element tuple needs a trailing comma: '(10,)'; '(10)' is just an int. Supports indexing, slicing, concatenation, repetition, packing/unpacking ('a, b = (1, 2)') and methods count() and index().

cards.title: Sets
cards.body: A set is an unordered collection of unique, hashable elements in curly braces: '{10, 20, 30}'. Duplicates are dropped, there is no indexing, and an empty set must be created with 'set()' because '{}' makes an empty dict. Methods: add(x), update(iterable), remove(x) (KeyError if absent), discard(x) (silent), pop(), clear(), copy(). Handy for removing duplicates: 'list(set(lst))'.

cards.title: Set Operations
cards.body: Mathematical operations: union 'a | b' or a.union(b); intersection 'a & b'; difference 'a - b'; symmetric difference 'a ^ b'; tests issubset(), issuperset(), isdisjoint(). Example: '{1, 2, 3} | {3, 4}' gives {1, 2, 3, 4}. A frozenset is an immutable set that can itself be a dictionary key or set member.

quiz.question: How do you create an empty set in Python?
quiz.explanation: '{}' creates an empty dictionary. Only set() creates an empty set.

cards.title: Dictionary Characteristics (Part 1)
cards.body: A dictionary stores key-value pairs in curly braces: 'stu = {101: "Rahul", 102: "Raj"}'. Keys must be unique and immutable (int, str, tuple); values can be anything and can repeat.

cards.title: Dictionary Characteristics (Part 2)
cards.body: Dictionaries are mutable and, since Python 3.7, preserve insertion order. Access with 'stu[101]' (KeyError if missing), add or change with 'stu[104] = "Sonam"', delete with 'del stu[102]', and test keys with '101 in stu'.

cards.title: Dictionary Methods
cards.body: get(key, default) returns a default instead of raising KeyError; keys(), values(), items() return views for looping ('for k, v in d.items()'); update(other) merges pairs; pop(key, default) removes and returns a value; popitem() removes the last inserted pair; setdefault(key, value) returns the value, inserting it if the key is absent; fromkeys(keys, value) builds a dict; clear(); copy().

cards.title: Nested Dicts & Comprehension
cards.body: Dictionaries can hold other dictionaries: 'a = {1: {"course": "Python", "fees": 15000}}' accessed as 'a[1]["fees"]'. Dictionary comprehension builds one in a line: '{n: n*n for n in range(5)}' gives {0: 0, 1: 1, 2: 4, 3: 9, 4: 16}.

quiz.question: What does d.get('x') return if the key 'x' is not in the dictionary d?
quiz.explanation: get() returns None (or a default you provide) instead of raising KeyError like d['x'] would.

cards.title: Mutable vs Immutable
cards.body: Mutable objects can be changed in place: list, set, dict (and array). Immutable objects cannot: int, float, bool, str, tuple, frozenset. This affects function arguments (mutable objects can be modified by the function) and what can be used as dictionary keys or set members (only immutable/hashable ones).

cards.title: When to Use What
cards.body: Array: many values of one numeric type, memory-efficient. List: ordered, changeable, mixed items. Tuple: fixed record that should not change. Set: unique items and fast membership tests. Dictionary: look up values by a meaningful key. Pick the simplest structure that matches how you access the data.

cards.title: Useful Built-in Functions for Collections
cards.body: len(), min(), max(), sum(), sorted(), reversed(), enumerate() (index + item), zip() (pair up sequences), any(), all(), id(), type(), 'sys.getsizeof()' (size in bytes), plus constructors int(), float(), str(), list(), tuple(), set(), dict() that also convert between types.

quiz.question: Which of these data types is immutable?
quiz.explanation: Tuples cannot be changed after creation. Lists, sets and dictionaries are mutable.

cards.title: The array Module (Part 1)
cards.body: 'import array' then 'a = array.array("i", [101, 102, 103])' creates an array that stores only one type, chosen by a type code: 'b'/'B' (signed/unsigned char), 'h'/'H' (short), 'i'/'I' (int), 'l'/'L' (long), 'q'/'Q' (long long), 'f' (float), 'd' (double).

cards.title: The array Module (Part 2)
cards.body: It uses less memory than a list and supports append, insert, pop, remove, index, reverse, extend, slicing and loops; adding the wrong type raises TypeError.

cards.title: NumPy Arrays
cards.body: NumPy ('import numpy as np') provides the ndarray, a fast n-dimensional array. Create with np.array([...]), np.arange(1, 10, 2), np.linspace(1, 8, 5), np.zeros((3, 2)), np.ones(5), and reshape with 'a.reshape(2, 3)'. Attributes: ndim, shape, size, dtype, itemsize, nbytes. Python has no built-in multi-dimensional array; NumPy fills that gap.

cards.title: Vectorized Operations
cards.body: NumPy applies operations to every element without loops: 'a + 5', 'a * b' (same shape), np.sum(a), np.prod(a), np.sqrt(a). Comparing arrays gives a boolean array ('a == b'); 'np.where(a > b, a, b)' picks element-wise; 'np.nonzero(a)' returns indexes of non-zero items; slicing works per dimension: 'a[0:2, 1:3]'.

cards.title: Alias, View & Copy
cards.body: 'b = a' is an alias (same object). 'b = a.view()' is a new array object that shares the same data, so changing one changes the other. 'b = a.copy()' duplicates the data, so the arrays are independent. 'flatten()' converts any array to 1-D and returns a copy.

quiz.question: What does np.arange(1, 10, 2) produce?
quiz.explanation: arange(start, stop, step) counts from 1 in steps of 2 and stops before 10: 1, 3, 5, 7, 9.

cards.title: The re Module
cards.body: A regular expression (regex) describes a text pattern. 'import re' gives: re.match(p, s) (match at the start only), re.search(p, s) (first match anywhere), re.findall(p, s) (list of all matches), re.finditer(), re.sub(p, repl, s) (replace), re.split(p, s), re.compile(p) (reuse a pattern). A match object offers group(), start(), end(), span(). Always write patterns as raw strings: r'\d+'.

cards.title: Pattern Syntax
cards.body: '.' any character, '^' start, '$' end, '*' zero or more, '+' one or more, '?' optional, '{n,m}' between n and m repeats, '[abc]' a character set, '[^abc]' not in set, '|' or, '()' groups. Shorthands: \d digit, \w word character, \s whitespace, \b word boundary (capitals negate: \D, \W, \S). Add '?' for lazy matching ('.*?'). Flag: re.IGNORECASE.

cards.title: Regex in Practice
cards.body: Extract numbers: 're.findall(r"\d+", "Order 12, item 7")' gives ['12', '7']. Validate an Indian mobile number: 're.fullmatch(r"[6-9]\d{9}", num)'. A simple email check: 're.match(r"^[\w.]+@[\w.]+\.\w+$", email)'. Clean text: 're.sub(r"\s+", " ", text)' collapses repeated spaces.

quiz.question: What does re.findall(r'\d+', 'a1b22c333') return?
quiz.explanation: findall returns all non-overlapping matches as strings: every run of digits is one match.

modules.title: Conditional Statements & Loops
modules.description: Decision making with if / elif / else and repetition with while and for loops, including nested structures and break, continue and pass.

cards.title: if and if-else
cards.body: 'if condition:' runs its indented block only when the condition is truthy; 'else:' runs otherwise. Example: 'if age >= 18: print("Adult") else: print("Minor")'. Conditions can combine comparisons with 'and', 'or', 'not'. The colon and consistent indentation are mandatory.

cards.title: if-elif-else & Nested if
cards.body: For several mutually exclusive cases use 'if ... elif ... elif ... else'; Python checks top to bottom and runs only the first true branch, so put specific cases first. An if inside another if is a nested if, useful for dependent checks (e.g. check login, then check role), but flatten with 'and' when possible to keep code readable.

cards.title: Ternary & match-case
cards.body: Short decisions fit in one line: 'msg = "even" if n % 2 == 0 else "odd"'. Python 3.10 added 'match-case' (structural pattern matching) as a cleaner alternative for many-way branching: 'match day: case "Sat" | "Sun": ... case _: ...' where '_' is the default.

quiz.question: Which keyword is Python's version of 'else if'?
quiz.explanation: Python uses the single keyword elif to chain additional conditions.

cards.title: The while Loop
cards.body: 'while condition:' repeats its block as long as the condition stays true, so something inside must eventually make it false (e.g. 'i += 1') or you create an infinite loop. 'while True:' with a 'break' is a common pattern for menus and input validation. A loop can have an 'else' block that runs when the condition becomes false normally (not when 'break' is used).

cards.title: The range() Function
cards.body: 'range(stop)', 'range(start, stop)' and 'range(start, stop, step)' generate integer sequences; stop is excluded, start defaults to 0 and step to 1. Examples: range(5) gives 0-4; range(1, 10, 2) gives 1, 3, 5, 7, 9; range(10, 0, -1) counts down from 10 to 1. Arguments must be integers and step cannot be 0. range is lazy; wrap it in list() to see the values.

quiz.question: What does list(range(2, 10, 3)) produce?
quiz.explanation: Start at 2, add 3 each time, and stop before 10: 2, 5, 8.

cards.title: The for Loop
cards.body: 'for item in iterable:' visits each element of a string, list, tuple, set, dictionary (keys) or range. Handy helpers: 'enumerate(lst)' gives (index, item) pairs, 'zip(a, b)' walks two sequences together, 'd.items()' gives key-value pairs. Like while, a for loop may have an 'else' block that runs if the loop finished without 'break'.

cards.title: Nested Loops
cards.body: A loop inside another loop: the inner loop completes all its iterations for each iteration of the outer loop. Typical uses: multiplication tables ('for i in range(1, 4): for j in range(1, 4): print(i*j, end=" ")'), star patterns (outer loop = rows, inner loop = columns), and traversing 2-D lists. Total runs = outer count x inner count.

quiz.question: How many times does print() run in: for i in range(3): for j in range(2): print(i, j)?
quiz.explanation: The inner loop runs 2 times for each of the 3 outer iterations, giving 3 x 2 = 6.

cards.title: break and continue
cards.body: 'break' immediately exits the nearest enclosing loop (and skips the loop's else block). 'continue' skips the rest of the current iteration and jumps to the next one. Example: 'for n in range(10): if n % 2 == 0: continue; print(n)' prints only odd numbers; 'if n == 7: break' would stop the loop entirely at 7.

cards.title: pass Statement
cards.body: 'pass' does nothing. It is a placeholder where Python needs a statement syntactically, such as an empty function, class, or if-branch you will fill in later: 'def todo(): pass'. Unlike 'continue', it does not alter loop flow.

cards.title: Loop else Example
cards.body: The for-else pattern is useful for searches: 'for i in range(2, n): if n % i == 0: print("Not prime"); break; else: print("Prime")'. The else block runs only if the loop completed without hitting 'break'.

quiz.question: What does the pass statement do?
quiz.explanation: pass is a no-operation statement used where a block is syntactically required but no action is needed yet.

modules.title: Functions in Python
modules.description: Defining and calling functions, all argument types, built-in functions, variable scope, plus lambda, recursion, generators and decorators.

cards.title: Why Functions?
cards.body: A function is a named block of code that performs a task. Benefits: write once and reuse, break big problems into small testable parts, easier maintenance and debugging. Python has built-in functions (print, len, sum) and user-defined functions you create with 'def'.

cards.title: Function Definition & Calling
cards.body: Syntax: 'def add(x, y): """Add two numbers""" return x + y'. The body must be indented. A function runs only when called: 'result = add(10, 20)'. Parameters have no declared types (dynamic typing). 'return' sends a value back; 'return a, b' returns a tuple that you can unpack ('s, d = calc(5)'); with no return, the function returns None.

quiz.question: What does a Python function return if it has no return statement?
quiz.explanation: Without an explicit return, a function returns None.

cards.title: Positional & Keyword Arguments
cards.body: Formal arguments are the parameters in the definition; actual arguments are the values in the call. Positional arguments match by order: 'pw(2, 5)' is not 'pw(5, 2)'. Keyword arguments match by name so order does not matter: 'show(age=62, name="Raj")'. Positional arguments must come before keyword ones, and the count must match or Python raises TypeError.

cards.title: Default Arguments
cards.body: Give a parameter a default value: 'def show(name, age=27)'. If the caller omits it, the default is used. Default parameters must come after non-default ones. Defaults are evaluated once, so never use a mutable default like 'lst=[]'; use 'lst=None' and create the list inside the function.

cards.title: Variable-Length Arguments
cards.body: '*args' collects any number of extra positional arguments into a tuple: 'def add(*nums): return sum(nums)'. '**kwargs' collects extra keyword arguments into a dictionary: 'def info(**data): ...' called as 'info(a=1, b=2)'. Order in a definition: normal, default, *args, keyword-only, **kwargs. At call time, '*' and '**' also unpack: 'add(*[1, 2, 3])'.

quiz.question: Where does *args store the extra positional arguments it receives?
quiz.explanation: *args packs the extra positional arguments into a tuple; **kwargs packs keyword arguments into a dictionary.

cards.title: Commonly Used Built-ins
cards.body: print, input, len, type, id, range, sum, min, max, sorted, abs, round, pow, divmod, enumerate, zip, any, all, isinstance, dir, help. Functional helpers: 'map(f, it)' applies f to every item, 'filter(f, it)' keeps items where f is true, and 'functools.reduce(f, it)' folds a sequence into one value. Example: 'list(map(lambda x: x * 2, [1, 2, 3]))' gives [2, 4, 6].

cards.title: The math Module
cards.body: 'import math' unlocks: floor(n) (round down), ceil(n) (round up), fabs(n), factorial(n), sqrt(n), pow(n, m), gcd(a, b), sin/cos/tan, log, and constants math.pi and math.e. Examples: math.ceil(4.2) = 5, math.floor(-4.2) = -5, math.factorial(5) = 120.

quiz.question: What is math.ceil(4.2)?
quiz.explanation: ceil rounds up to the next integer, so 4.2 becomes 5.

cards.title: Local & Global Variables
cards.body: A variable created inside a function is local: it exists only during the call and is invisible outside. A variable created at the top level is global and readable everywhere below it. Python resolves names with the LEGB rule: Local, Enclosing, Global, Built-in. If a local and a global share a name, the local shadows the global inside the function.

cards.title: global & nonlocal
cards.body: To assign to a global variable inside a function, declare 'global count' first; otherwise Python treats the assignment as creating a new local. 'nonlocal' does the same for a variable in an enclosing function (nested functions). 'globals()' returns a dictionary of all global names. Prefer passing arguments and returning values over global state.

cards.title: Call by Object Reference
cards.body: Python passes references to objects (neither pure pass-by-value nor pass-by-reference). If the object is immutable (int, str, tuple) and the function 'changes' it, a new object is created and the caller is unaffected. If it is mutable (list, dict), changes like 'lst.append(4)' are visible to the caller. Re-assigning the parameter to a brand-new list inside the function does not affect the caller.

quiz.question: A function does 'lst.append(4)' on a list parameter. What happens to the caller's list?
quiz.explanation: Lists are mutable and passed by object reference, so in-place changes are visible outside the function.

cards.title: Lambda (Anonymous) Functions
cards.body: A lambda is a small nameless function: 'lambda x, y: x + y'. It holds exactly one expression (no statements) and returns its value automatically. Common use: as an argument, e.g. 'sorted(names, key=lambda s: len(s))' or 'filter(lambda n: n % 2 == 0, nums)'. Call immediately with '(lambda x: x + 1)(5)'.

cards.title: Recursion
cards.body: A recursive function calls itself. It needs a base case that stops the recursion and a recursive case that moves toward it: 'def fact(n): return 1 if n <= 1 else n * fact(n - 1)'. Python limits depth to about 1000 calls ('sys.getrecursionlimit()'); exceeding it raises RecursionError, so use loops for very deep problems.

cards.title: Generators
cards.body: A generator function uses 'yield' instead of 'return' and produces values one at a time, remembering its state between calls: 'def count(n): for i in range(n): yield i'. Retrieve values with 'next(gen)' or a for loop. Generators are memory-efficient for large or endless sequences.

cards.title: Decorators
cards.body: A decorator takes a function and returns an enhanced version without modifying its code. Apply it with '@name' above the definition: 'def log(f): def wrapper(*a, **k): print("calling", f.__name__); return f(*a, **k); return wrapper' then '@log def hello(): ...'. Used for logging, timing, access control (Django's @login_required is a decorator).

quiz.question: Which keyword turns a function into a generator?
quiz.explanation: A function containing yield returns a generator object that produces values lazily.

modules.title: File Processing
modules.description: Opening, reading, writing and closing files, file modes, and the key file-handling functions.

cards.title: Concept of Files
cards.body: A file is a named place on disk for storing data permanently, unlike variables which vanish when the program ends. Text files hold readable characters; binary files hold raw bytes (images, PDFs). Paths can be relative ('data.txt') or absolute ('C:/proj/data.txt' or '/home/user/data.txt'). Python works with a file through a file object returned by open().

cards.title: open() and File Modes
cards.body: 'f = open(filename, mode)'. Modes: 'r' read (default; error if missing), 'w' write (creates or erases existing content), 'a' append (adds at the end), 'x' create (error if exists), 'r+' read and write, 'w+' and 'a+' read/write variants. Add 'b' for binary ('rb', 'wb') or 't' for text. Specify 'encoding="utf-8"' for text files.

cards.title: close() and the with Statement
cards.body: Always close a file with 'f.close()' so buffered data is flushed and resources are released. The safer way is the context manager: 'with open("a.txt", "w") as f: f.write("Hi")' closes the file automatically, even if an error occurs. Missing files raise FileNotFoundError, which you can handle with try/except.

quiz.question: Which file mode adds new content at the end without erasing existing content?
quiz.explanation: 'a' (append) preserves existing data and writes at the end. 'w' would erase the file first.

cards.title: Reading from a File
cards.body: 'f.read()' returns the whole content as one string ('f.read(10)' reads 10 characters); 'f.readline()' returns one line (including the newline); 'f.readlines()' returns a list of all lines. The most memory-friendly way is to loop: 'for line in f: print(line.strip())'. Reading past the end returns an empty string.

cards.title: Writing to a File
cards.body: 'f.write(text)' writes a string and returns the number of characters written; it does not add a newline, so include '\n' yourself. 'f.writelines(list_of_strings)' writes many strings (again no automatic newlines). Mode 'w' erases existing content first. 'f.flush()' forces buffered data to disk; 'print("x", file=f)' also writes to a file.

cards.title: File Pointer & Other Functions
cards.body: 'f.tell()' returns the current position and 'f.seek(offset)' moves it ('f.seek(0)' rewinds). Attributes: f.name, f.mode, f.closed. The os module helps manage files: 'os.path.exists(p)', 'os.remove(p)', 'os.rename(a, b)', 'os.listdir(folder)', 'os.getcwd()'. For binary files use 'rb'/'wb', e.g. copying an image byte by byte.

quiz.question: Which method reads exactly one line from a file?
quiz.explanation: readline() returns the next single line. readlines() returns all lines as a list, and read() returns the entire content.

modules.title: Modules
modules.description: Modularization, importing modules, creating your own, and a tour of Python's built-in modules.

cards.title: Concept of Modularization (Part 1)
cards.body: A module is simply a .py file containing functions, classes and variables that other programs can reuse; a package is a folder of modules (with an '__init__.py').

cards.title: Concept of Modularization (Part 2)
cards.body: Modularization splits a large program into small, focused files, giving code reuse, separate namespaces (no name clashes), easier teamwork, testing and maintenance. Sources: the standard library, third-party packages installed with pip, and your own files.

cards.title: Ways to Import
cards.body: 'import math' (use 'math.sqrt(9)'), 'import math as m' (alias), 'from math import sqrt, pi' (use 'sqrt(9)' directly), 'from math import *' (imports everything; discouraged because of name clashes). Explore a module with 'dir(math)' and 'help(math.sqrt)'. Python searches the current folder, then 'sys.path' locations.

cards.title: Creating Your Own Module
cards.body: Save 'def add(a, b): return a + b' as 'calc.py', then in another file in the same folder write 'import calc; print(calc.add(2, 3))'. Use 'if __name__ == "__main__":' in a module to put code that runs only when the file is executed directly, not when imported. Python caches compiled modules in '__pycache__'.

quiz.question: Which statement imports only the sqrt function from the math module?
quiz.explanation: The 'from module import name' form imports a specific name so you can call it directly as sqrt().

cards.title: Popular Standard Library Modules
cards.body: math (maths functions), random (random numbers), datetime (dates and times), os (operating system and paths), sys (interpreter details, command-line args), time (delays, timestamps), json (read/write JSON), re (regular expressions), collections (Counter, deque, defaultdict), statistics (mean, median). They ship with Python, so no installation is required.

cards.title: Demo: random and datetime
cards.body: 'import random': 'random.randint(1, 6)' gives a dice roll (both ends inclusive), 'random.choice(items)' picks one item, 'random.shuffle(lst)' shuffles in place. 'from datetime import datetime, timedelta': 'datetime.now()' is the current time, 'datetime.now().strftime("%d-%m-%Y")' formats it, and 'now + timedelta(days=7)' gives the date a week later.

cards.title: Third-Party Modules with pip
cards.body: Packages not in the standard library come from PyPI via pip: 'pip install requests', 'pip uninstall requests', 'pip list', 'pip --version'. Then 'import requests' like any module. Install inside a virtual environment (venv or conda) to keep project dependencies separate.

quiz.question: Which module would you use to generate a random dice roll?
quiz.explanation: random.randint(1, 6) returns a random integer from 1 to 6 inclusive.

units.title: Module 7: Python OOPs
units.description: Object-oriented Python: classes and objects, the four pillars (encapsulation, inheritance, polymorphism, abstraction), and robust exception handling.

modules.title: OOP Concepts, Classes & Objects
modules.description: Why object-oriented programming exists, and how to model real things with classes, objects, constructors, destructors, and static/class methods.

cards.title: What is OOP?
cards.body: Object-Oriented Programming organizes a program around objects that bundle data (attributes) with the behaviour that works on that data (methods), instead of a loose collection of functions. It models real-world entities such as a Student, Car or BankAccount. Python supports procedural and object-oriented styles, and in fact everything in Python (ints, strings, functions) is an object.

cards.title: Key OOP Principles
cards.body: Four pillars: Encapsulation (bundling data and methods and restricting direct access), Abstraction (exposing what an object does while hiding how), Inheritance (a child class reuses and extends a parent class), and Polymorphism (the same interface behaving differently for different objects).

cards.title: Advantages of OOP
cards.body: Code organization: related data and logic live together in one class. Reusability: inheritance and composition avoid rewriting code. Modularity: each class is a self-contained unit. Scalability: new features are added as new classes without breaking old ones. Maintainability: a bug or change is localised to one class, which makes large projects (like Django itself) manageable.

quiz.question: Which of the following is NOT one of the four pillars of OOP?
quiz.explanation: The four pillars are encapsulation, abstraction, inheritance and polymorphism. Compilation is not an OOP concept.

cards.title: Defining a Class
cards.body: A class is a blueprint that defines attributes (data) and methods (functions). Syntax: 'class Student: def __init__(self, name, age): self.name = name; self.age = age' and 'def show(self): print(self.name, self.age)'. Class names use PascalCase. Every instance method takes 'self' as the first parameter, which refers to the object the method is called on. An empty class can use 'pass'.

cards.title: Creating Objects
cards.body: An object is an instance of a class: 's1 = Student("Asha", 21)'. Each object has its own copy of instance attributes ('s1.name', 's2.name' are independent), and calls methods with dot notation: 's1.show()'. Python passes 's1' to 'self' automatically. Useful tools: type(s1), isinstance(s1, Student), s1.__dict__ (attribute dictionary), dir(s1).

cards.title: Instance vs Class Attributes
cards.body: Instance attributes are set via 'self.x' (usually in __init__) and belong to one object. Class attributes are defined directly in the class body and are shared by all instances: 'class Student: college = "NIT"'. Read them through the class or an instance ('Student.college'); change a shared value through the class, because assigning via an instance creates a new instance attribute that shadows it.

quiz.question: What does 'self' refer to inside an instance method?
options: The current object calling the method
quiz.explanation: self is the instance on which the method was called, giving the method access to that object's attributes.

cards.title: Constructors (__init__) (Part 1)
cards.body: '__init__' is the constructor: Python calls it automatically right after an object is created, to initialise its attributes. It can take parameters ('Student("Asha", 21)') and default values ('def __init__(self, name, age=18)').

cards.title: Constructors (__init__) (Part 2)
cards.body: Python does not support multiple constructors by overloading; use default arguments, *args, or a class method as an alternative constructor. A constructor must not return a value.

cards.title: Destructors (__del__)
cards.body: '__del__' is called when an object is about to be destroyed, i.e. when its reference count drops to zero (for example after 'del obj' or when it goes out of scope). Python's garbage collector manages memory, and the exact timing of __del__ is not guaranteed, so use it only for light clean-up; prefer 'with' statements (context managers) for closing files or connections.

cards.title: Instance, Class & Static Methods (Part 1)
cards.body: Instance methods take 'self' and work with one object's data. '@classmethod' methods take 'cls' and work with class-level data or act as alternative constructors: 'def from_string(cls, s): name, age = s.split("-"); return cls(name, int(age))'.

cards.title: Instance, Class & Static Methods (Part 2)
cards.body: '@staticmethod' methods take neither self nor cls; they are utility functions grouped inside the class: 'def is_adult(age): return age >= 18'. Call class and static methods on the class: 'Student.is_adult(20)'.

quiz.question: Which decorator marks a method that receives the class (cls) as its first argument?
quiz.explanation: @classmethod passes the class as cls. @staticmethod passes nothing automatically.

cards.title: What are Dunder Methods?
cards.body: Methods with double underscores on both sides (__init__, __str__, __len__) are special methods, also called magic or dunder methods. You rarely call them directly; Python calls them when you use built-in syntax: 'str(obj)' calls __str__, 'len(obj)' calls __len__, 'obj[0]' calls __getitem__, 'a == b' calls __eq__. Defining them makes your classes behave like built-in types.

cards.title: __str__ vs __repr__ (Part 1)
cards.body: __str__ returns a readable message for end users and is used by print() and str(). __repr__ returns an unambiguous developer-friendly string (ideally one that looks like the constructor call) and is used in the shell, in debugging, and when objects are shown inside lists.

cards.title: __str__ vs __repr__ (Part 2)
cards.body: If only __repr__ is defined, print() falls back to it. Example: 'def __repr__(self): return f"Student({self.name!r}, {self.age})"'.

cards.title: Comparison, Length & Container Methods (Part 1)
cards.body: __eq__ (==), __ne__ (!=), __lt__ (<), __le__, __gt__, __ge__ enable comparison and sorting of your objects ('@functools.total_ordering' fills in the rest from __eq__ and one ordering method).

cards.title: Comparison, Length & Container Methods (Part 2)
cards.body: __len__ powers len(), __getitem__ enables indexing and slicing, __iter__ makes the object usable in for loops, __contains__ powers 'in', and __call__ makes an object callable like a function. If you define __eq__, also define __hash__ if the object must be used in sets or as a dict key.

quiz.question: Which special method does print(obj) call to get a readable string?
quiz.explanation: print() uses __str__. If __str__ is not defined, Python falls back to __repr__.

cards.title: Shared State with Class Variables (Part 1)
cards.body: A class variable is shared by every instance, which makes it perfect for counters and constants: 'class Employee: count = 0' with '__init__' doing 'Employee.count += 1'.

cards.title: Shared State with Class Variables (Part 2)
cards.body: Always update it via the class name ('Employee.count'), because 'self.count += 1' would create a new instance attribute instead. Warning: a mutable class attribute such as 'items = []' is shared by all objects; create such lists inside __init__ via 'self.items = []'.

cards.title: Inspecting Objects (Part 1)
cards.body: Python lets you examine objects at run time: 'type(o)' gives the class, 'isinstance(o, C)' tests the type, 'o.__dict__' lists instance attributes, 'dir(o)' lists all attributes and methods, 'hasattr(o, "x")' checks, 'getattr(o, "x", default)' reads, 'setattr(o, "x", v)' writes, 'delattr(o, "x")' deletes.

cards.title: Inspecting Objects (Part 2)
cards.body: 'o.__class__.__name__' gives the class name as a string. Frameworks like Django use these heavily.

cards.title: Object Identity & Copying
cards.body: Assigning 'b = a' makes both names point to one object.
