'copy.copy(a)' creates a shallow copy (new object, but nested objects are shared) and 'copy.deepcopy(a)' copies everything recursively. 'id(a)' reveals identity, and '==' compares values (calls __eq__) while 'is' compares identity. Remember that custom objects are mutable: changing an attribute through one name is visible through all names.

quiz.question: Why should a class counter be updated as 'Employee.count += 1' rather than 'self.count += 1'?
options: self.count is not allowed in Python
self.count += 1 creates a new instance attribute instead of updating the shared one
It makes the code run faster
quiz.explanation: Assigning through self creates an instance attribute that shadows the class variable, so the shared counter stays unchanged.

modules.title: Encapsulation, Inheritance, Polymorphism & Abstraction
modules.description: The four pillars in Python: protecting data, reusing classes through every inheritance type, overriding and overloading behaviour, and defining abstract interfaces.

cards.title: Access Levels & Name Mangling (Part 1)
cards.body: Encapsulation hides internal state so it is changed only through controlled methods.

cards.title: Access Levels & Name Mangling (Part 2)
cards.body: Python uses naming conventions: 'name' is public; '_name' is protected by convention (internal use, meant for subclasses); '__name' is private via name mangling, so 'self.__balance' becomes '_Account__balance' and cannot be accessed as 'acc.__balance' from outside. Python trusts programmers: private is a strong hint, not a lock.

cards.title: Getters, Setters & @property (Part 1)
cards.body: Expose data safely through methods that can validate input. The Pythonic way is '@property': 'class Account: def __init__(self, b): self.__balance = b' then '@property def balance(self): return self.__balance' and '@balance.setter def balance(self, v): if v < 0: raise ValueError("negative"); self.__balance = v'.

cards.title: Getters, Setters & @property (Part 2)
cards.body: Users still write 'acc.balance = 500', but validation runs. Omit the setter to make the attribute read-only.

quiz.question: Inside class Account, the attribute self.__balance is stored (name-mangled) as:
quiz.explanation: Python rewrites a double-underscore attribute to _ClassName__attribute to avoid accidental access and clashes.

cards.title: Single & Multilevel Inheritance
cards.body: Inheritance lets a child (derived) class reuse the attributes and methods of a parent (base) class: 'class Dog(Animal):'. Single: one parent, one child. Multilevel: a chain, e.g. 'class C(B)' where 'class B(A)', so C inherits from both B and A. Check relationships with 'isinstance(obj, Animal)' and 'issubclass(Dog, Animal)'. Every class ultimately inherits from 'object'.

cards.title: Multiple, Hierarchical & Hybrid
cards.body: Multiple: one child, many parents: 'class C(A, B)'. Hierarchical: one parent, many children ('class Dog(Animal)' and 'class Cat(Animal)'). Hybrid: a mix of these, such as the diamond where B and C both inherit A and D inherits B and C. Python resolves which method to run using the Method Resolution Order (MRO, C3 linearization); inspect it with 'D.__mro__' or 'D.mro()'.

cards.title: super() & Method Overriding
cards.body: A child can redefine a parent method with the same name (method overriding) and the child's version is used for child objects. 'super()' calls the parent's version: 'class Student(Person): def __init__(self, name, roll): super().__init__(name); self.roll = roll'. In multiple inheritance, super() follows the MRO, so it enables cooperative calls through every class in the chain.

quiz.question: Which attribute or method shows the order in which Python searches parent classes?
quiz.explanation: ClassName.__mro__ (or ClassName.mro()) lists the Method Resolution Order Python uses to look up methods.

cards.title: Method Overriding & Duck Typing (Part 1)
cards.body: Polymorphism means 'many forms': the same call behaves differently by object type. With overriding, 'shape.area()' runs Circle's or Rectangle's version depending on the object.

cards.title: Method Overriding & Duck Typing (Part 2)
cards.body: Python also uses duck typing: it does not care about the class, only that the object has the needed method ('if it walks like a duck and quacks like a duck, it is a duck'). Built-ins show it too: 'len()' works on strings, lists and dicts.

cards.title: Method Overloading in Python
cards.body: Python does not support classic method overloading: if you define two methods with the same name, the last definition replaces the earlier ones. Simulate it with default arguments ('def area(self, a, b=None)'), '*args', or type checks inside one method.

cards.title: Operator Overloading
cards.body: Special 'dunder' methods let your objects work with operators: __add__ (+), __sub__ (-), __mul__ (*), __eq__ (==), __lt__ (<), __len__ (len()), __str__ (print/str()), __repr__ (debugging). Example: 'class Vec: def __add__(self, o): return Vec(self.x + o.x, self.y + o.y)' lets you write 'v1 + v2'. This is why '+' adds numbers but also joins strings.

quiz.question: Which special method is called when you use the + operator on two custom objects?
quiz.explanation: Defining __add__ in a class customises the + operator for its objects.

cards.title: Abstract Classes & Methods (Part 1)
cards.body: Abstraction exposes the essential interface and hides the details. Python provides it through the abc module: 'from abc import ABC, abstractmethod' then 'class Shape(ABC): @abstractmethod def area(self): pass'.

cards.title: Abstract Classes & Methods (Part 2)
cards.body: An abstract class cannot be instantiated ('Shape()' raises TypeError), and any subclass must implement all abstract methods before it can be instantiated. Abstract classes may also include normal (concrete) methods.

cards.title: Abstraction Example
cards.body: 'class Circle(Shape): def __init__(self, r): self.r = r' with 'def area(self): return 3.14159 * self.r ** 2' and 'class Rectangle(Shape)' with its own area(). Code can then work with any Shape through 'shape.area()' without caring about the concrete type, combining abstraction with polymorphism. Frameworks use this to define contracts that your classes must follow.

quiz.question: What happens if you try to create an object of a class that has an unimplemented @abstractmethod?
quiz.explanation: Abstract classes cannot be instantiated until all their abstract methods are implemented by a subclass.

cards.title: Is-A vs Has-A
cards.body: Inheritance models an 'is-a' relationship (a Dog is an Animal). Composition models 'has-a': a Car has an Engine, so the Car class creates and holds an Engine object: 'class Car: def __init__(self): self.engine = Engine()'. Car calls 'self.engine.start()' to delegate work. Composition is more flexible than inheritance because parts can be swapped without changing the class hierarchy.

cards.title: Aggregation vs Composition
cards.body: In composition the part cannot exist without the whole and is created inside it (a House and its Rooms). In aggregation the whole only references parts that live independently and are passed in: 'class Department: def __init__(self, employees): self.employees = employees' (employees outlive the department). Both are done by storing objects as attributes; the difference is lifecycle and ownership.

cards.title: Prefer Composition Over Inheritance
cards.body: A common design rule: use inheritance only for a true is-a relationship with shared behaviour; otherwise compose. Deep inheritance chains are brittle because a change in a base class ripples through all subclasses. Example: instead of 'class Logger(FileWriter)', give Logger a writer object ('self.writer = writer') so you can plug in a file writer, console writer or network writer.

quiz.question: A Car class creates and stores its own Engine object. Which relationship is this?
quiz.explanation: Holding another object as an attribute is composition ('has-a'). Inheritance would be 'is-a'.

cards.title: Mixins
cards.body: A mixin is a small class that provides one reusable behaviour and is not meant to stand alone: 'class JsonMixin: def to_json(self): import json; return json.dumps(self.__dict__)'. Add it to any class with multiple inheritance: 'class Student(JsonMixin, Person): ...'. Mixins share optional features across unrelated classes without building a deep hierarchy.

cards.title: The Diamond Problem
cards.body: If B and C both inherit A and D inherits (B, C), a method defined in A, B and C raises the question: which one does D use? Python solves it with the C3 MRO: D, B, C, A, object (children before parents, and left-to-right order of bases is kept). With cooperative 'super().method()' calls in each class, every version runs exactly once. Check the order with 'D.__mro__'.

cards.title: Dataclasses
cards.body: The @dataclass decorator (module 'dataclasses') auto-generates __init__, __repr__ and __eq__ for classes that mainly store data: 'from dataclasses import dataclass' then '@dataclass class Point: x: int; y: int = 0'. Options: 'frozen=True' makes instances immutable, and mutable defaults need 'field(default_factory=list)'. It removes boilerplate code from simple model classes.

quiz.question: In the diamond hierarchy class D(B, C) where B and C both inherit from A, what is D's MRO?
quiz.explanation: C3 linearization keeps the order of listed bases (B before C) and puts a shared parent (A) after all its children.

modules.title: Error & Exception Handling
modules.description: Handling runtime errors gracefully with try, except, else and finally, raising exceptions, and building custom exceptions.

cards.title: Errors vs Exceptions
cards.body: A syntax error is caught before the program runs (e.g. a missing colon). An exception is a runtime error that stops the program unless handled. Common ones: ZeroDivisionError, ValueError (int('abc')), TypeError, IndexError, KeyError, NameError, AttributeError, FileNotFoundError, ImportError. All inherit from BaseException, mostly through Exception; the traceback shows where the error happened.

cards.title: try and except
cards.body: Put risky code in 'try' and handle failures in 'except': 'try: n = int(input()); print(10 / n) except ValueError: print("Enter a number") except ZeroDivisionError: print("Cannot divide by zero")'. Catch several types with a tuple ('except (TypeError, ValueError):') and capture the object with 'as e'. List specific exceptions before general ones, and avoid a bare 'except:' that hides bugs.

cards.title: else and finally
cards.body: 'else' runs only if the try block raised no exception, which keeps success-only code out of the try. 'finally' always runs, whether or not an exception occurred, even if there is a return, making it ideal for clean-up such as closing files or connections. Full order: try, then except (if error), else (if no error), finally (always).

quiz.question: Which block of a try statement always executes, whether or not an exception occurs?
quiz.explanation: finally runs in every case and is used for clean-up. else runs only when no exception occurred.

cards.title: raise and assert
cards.body: Trigger an exception yourself with 'raise ValueError("Age cannot be negative")'. Inside an except block, a bare 'raise' re-raises the current exception, and 'raise NewError("msg") from e' chains errors. 'assert condition, "message"' raises AssertionError if the condition is false, useful for checking assumptions while developing.

cards.title: Custom Exceptions
cards.body: Create your own exception by subclassing Exception: 'class InsufficientFundsError(Exception): def __init__(self, balance, amount): super().__init__(f"Balance {balance} is less than {amount}")'. Raise it where the rule is broken and catch it where you can respond. Name custom exceptions ending in 'Error', catch specific types, and never silently swallow errors.

cards.title: Putting It Together: Bank Account (Part 1)
cards.body: A mini model combining the module's ideas: 'class Account: def __init__(self, bal): self.__balance = bal' (encapsulation); '@property def balance(self): return self.__balance'

cards.title: Putting It Together: Bank Account (Part 2)
cards.body: 'def withdraw(self, amt): if amt > self.__balance: raise InsufficientFundsError(self.__balance, amt); self.__balance -= amt'. Caller: 'try: acc.withdraw(500) except InsufficientFundsError as e: print(e) finally: print("Transaction done")'.

quiz.question: How do you create a custom exception class in Python?
options: By defining a function named exception()
quiz.explanation: Custom exceptions are classes that inherit (directly or indirectly) from Exception.

cards.title: The Exception Hierarchy (Part 1)
cards.body: All exceptions derive from BaseException. Directly under it are SystemExit, KeyboardInterrupt (Ctrl+C) and Exception.

cards.title: The Exception Hierarchy (Part 2)
cards.body: Nearly everything you handle is a subclass of Exception: ArithmeticError (ZeroDivisionError, OverflowError), LookupError (IndexError, KeyError), OSError (FileNotFoundError, PermissionError), ValueError, TypeError, AttributeError, NameError, ImportError (ModuleNotFoundError), RuntimeError (RecursionError), StopIteration. Catching a parent class also catches all its children.

cards.title: Common Exceptions and Their Causes (Part 1)
cards.body: ZeroDivisionError: dividing by zero. ValueError: right type, wrong value ('int("abc")'). TypeError: wrong type ('"a" + 1'). IndexError: list index out of range. KeyError: missing dictionary key. AttributeError: object has no such attribute ('None.upper()').

cards.title: Common Exceptions and Their Causes (Part 2)
cards.body: NameError: undefined variable. FileNotFoundError: file path does not exist. ImportError/ModuleNotFoundError: module cannot be imported. Reading the traceback bottom-up shows the type and message first.

cards.title: EAFP vs LBYL
cards.body: Python style favours EAFP ('Easier to Ask Forgiveness than Permission'): try the operation and handle the exception, e.g. 'try: value = d[key] except KeyError: value = 0'. LBYL ('Look Before You Leap') checks first: 'if key in d: value = d[key]'. EAFP avoids race conditions (like a file deleted between the check and the open) and is often cleaner.

quiz.question: Which exception is raised when you access a missing key in a dictionary?
quiz.explanation: d['missing'] raises KeyError. IndexError is for sequences such as lists.

cards.title: Handling File Errors
cards.body: File operations fail often, so wrap them: 'try: with open("data.txt") as f: print(f.read()) except FileNotFoundError: print("File not found") except PermissionError: print("No permission")'. In Python 3, IOError is an alias of OSError, so 'except OSError' covers most file and system problems. Using 'with' guarantees the file closes even when an exception occurs.

cards.title: How the with Statement Works
cards.body: 'with' uses a context manager: an object with __enter__ (runs on entering, its return value goes to 'as') and __exit__ (always runs on leaving, even after an exception; returning True suppresses the exception). Besides files, it is used for database connections, locks and temporary settings. Multiple managers: 'with open(a) as f1, open(b, "w") as f2:'.

cards.title: Writing Your Own Context Manager
cards.body: Class-based: 'class Timer: def __enter__(self): self.t = time.time(); return self' and 'def __exit__(self, exc_type, exc, tb): print(time.time() - self.t)'. Function-based with contextlib: '@contextmanager def opened(p): f = open(p); try: yield f finally: f.close()'. Both let callers write 'with Timer():' and rely on guaranteed clean-up.

quiz.question: What is the main advantage of using the with statement for files?
options: It closes the file automatically, even if an error occurs
quiz.explanation: The context manager's __exit__ always runs, so the file is closed properly even when an exception is raised inside the block.

modules.title: OOP in Practice: Mini Projects & Best Practices
modules.description: Apply everything together: build small object-oriented systems, then learn the design habits and common mistakes that matter in real projects.

cards.title: Designing the Classes (Part 1)
cards.body: Start by listing nouns (Student, Course) and verbs (enrol, grade, report). 'class Student: def __init__(self, roll, name): self.roll = roll; self.name = name; self.marks = {}' stores marks per subject; 'def add_mark(self, subject, score): if not 0 <= score <= 100: raise ValueError("Score must be 0-100"); self.marks[subject] = score'.

cards.title: Designing the Classes (Part 2)
cards.body: 'def average(self): return sum(self.marks.values()) / len(self.marks) if self.marks else 0'.

cards.title: Composition and Reports
cards.body: 'class Course: def __init__(self, title): self.title = title; self.students = []' with 'def enrol(self, student): self.students.append(student)' (a Course has Students) and 'def topper(self): return max(self.students, key=lambda s: s.average())'. Add '__str__' to Student ('f"{self.roll} - {self.name}: {self.average():.1f}"') so 'print(student)' gives a clean report line.

cards.title: Adding Persistence
cards.body: Convert objects to dictionaries ('s.__dict__') and save them with 'json.dump' to a file; reload with 'json.load' and rebuild with 'Student(**data)'-style constructors or a '@classmethod from_dict(cls, d)'. Wrap file access in try/except so a missing or corrupt file does not crash the program. This is the same save/load idea Django models automate with a database.

quiz.question: In the Course/Student design, why does Course store a list of Student objects?
options: It is composition/aggregation: a Course has students
quiz.explanation: A Course 'has' students, so it keeps them as attributes: a has-a relationship rather than inheritance.

lessons.title: Mini Project: Library System with Inheritance & Exceptions

cards.title: Model & Custom Exceptions (Part 1)
cards.body: Classes: Book (title, isbn, available), Member (name, borrowed list), Library (books dict). Custom errors: 'class BookNotAvailableError(Exception): pass' and 'class LimitExceededError(Exception): pass'.

cards.title: Model & Custom Exceptions (Part 2)
cards.body: 'Library.lend(isbn, member)' looks up the book (raising KeyError for an unknown ISBN), checks 'book.available', raises BookNotAvailableError if it is out, then marks it unavailable and appends it to 'member.borrowed'.

cards.title: Inheritance & Polymorphism
cards.body: 'class Member: limit = 3' with 'def can_borrow(self): return len(self.borrowed) < self.limit'. 'class PremiumMember(Member): limit = 10' overrides the class attribute and the same 'can_borrow()' now behaves differently: polymorphism through overriding. 'class Librarian(Member)' could add 'add_book()'. Library code calls 'member.can_borrow()' without checking the member's type.

cards.title: Putting It Together
cards.body: Client code: 'try: lib.lend("101", asha) except BookNotAvailableError: print("Book is out") except LimitExceededError: print("Return a book first") except KeyError: print("Unknown ISBN") else: print("Issued") finally: print("Request processed")'. This exercises encapsulation (state hidden in classes), inheritance, polymorphism, custom exceptions and try/except/else/finally in one flow.

quiz.question: In the Library project, PremiumMember sets limit = 10 while Member has limit = 3. This is an example of:
options: Overriding an inherited attribute (specialisation through inheritance)
quiz.explanation: The subclass redefines an inherited class attribute, so the shared method can_borrow() behaves differently for premium members.

cards.title: Design Habits (Part 1)
cards.body: Give each class a single responsibility (a Student class should not also send emails). Keep classes small, name them with nouns in PascalCase and methods with verbs in snake_case.

cards.title: Design Habits (Part 2)
cards.body: Prefer composition to deep inheritance, use @property for validated attributes, add docstrings, define __repr__ for debugging, and rely on abstract base classes to define contracts. Keep inheritance chains shallow, ideally two or three levels.

cards.title: Common Mistakes (Part 1)
cards.body: 1) Forgetting 'self' in a method definition or call (TypeError: takes 0 positional arguments but 1 was given). 2) Forgetting 'super().__init__()' in a child constructor, so parent attributes are missing.

cards.title: Common Mistakes (Part 2)
cards.body: 3) Using a mutable default argument or mutable class attribute, which is shared. 4) Comparing objects with 'is' instead of '==' (and not defining __eq__). 5) Catching a broad 'except Exception: pass', which hides bugs.

cards.title: Why It Matters for Django
cards.body: Django is built on these ideas: models are classes (Model) with attributes as fields and instances as database rows; class-based views inherit from View; forms, admin and REST serializers all use inheritance, mixins, class methods and custom exceptions. Mastering classes, super(), @property and exception handling makes reading and extending Django code far easier.

quiz.question: A child class constructor omits the call to super().__init__(). What is the most likely result?
options: Python calls it automatically with no effect
Attributes set by the parent constructor are missing on the child object
quiz.explanation: Defining __init__ in the child replaces the parent's, so the parent's attribute setup does not run unless you call super().__init__().

units.title: Module 8: SQL Basics
units.description: Relational databases, connecting to MySQL, basic DML operations, query parameters and joins.

modules.title: Introduction to RDBMS
modules.description: Databases, relational model, keys, SQL categories, data types and creating tables.

cards.title: Database
cards.body: A database is an organised collection of data that is stored electronically so it can be easily accessed, managed and updated. Examples: a college's student records, a shop's products and orders, a bank's accounts.

cards.title: DBMS
cards.body: A Database Management System (DBMS) is software that lets you create, store, retrieve, update and delete data in a database. It also controls security, backup and multi-user access. Examples: MySQL, Oracle, PostgreSQL, SQL Server, SQLite.

cards.title: Why not Files?
cards.body: Plain files lead to duplicate data, inconsistent values, weak security and difficult searching. A DBMS solves these problems with structure, rules and fast queries.

quiz.question: What is a DBMS?
options: Software used to create, store and manage databases
quiz.explanation: A DBMS is software to create, store, retrieve, update and delete data, e.g. MySQL or Oracle.

cards.title: Relational Model
cards.body: A Relational Database Management System (RDBMS) stores data in tables (also called relations). Tables are connected to each other through common columns called keys. MySQL, Oracle, PostgreSQL and SQL Server are all RDBMS. The relational model was proposed by E. F. Codd in 1970.

cards.title: Table, Row, Column
cards.body: A table is a collection of related data. A row (also called a record or tuple) holds one entry, e.g. one student. A column (also called a field or attribute) holds one kind of information, e.g. the student's name. The number of rows is the cardinality and the number of columns is the degree of the table.

cards.title: Example Table: students
cards.body: students(id, name, city, dept_id): 1 - Rahul - Guwahati - 10; 2 - Rani - Delhi - 20; 3 - Sumit - Guwahati - 10; 4 - Anita - Pune - NULL. Each row is one student and each column is one property.

quiz.question: In an RDBMS, data is stored in...
options: Tables made of rows and columns
quiz.explanation: A relational database stores data in tables (relations) with rows and columns.

cards.title: Primary Key
cards.body: A primary key uniquely identifies every row in a table. It cannot be NULL and cannot repeat. Example: id in students. A table can have only one primary key (it may be made of several columns).

cards.title: Foreign Key
cards.body: A foreign key is a column that refers to the primary key of another table. It creates the link between tables. Example: students.dept_id refers to departments.dept_id. It also protects data integrity - you cannot add a student to a department that does not exist.

cards.title: Other Keys & Relationship Types
cards.body: Unique key: values must be different but one NULL is allowed. Candidate key: any column that could serve as primary key. Relationships: one-to-one, one-to-many (one department has many students) and many-to-many (students and courses, solved with a third linking table).

quiz.question: Which key links one table to another table?
quiz.explanation: A foreign key refers to the primary key of another table and creates the link.

cards.title: Structured Query Language
cards.body: SQL (Structured Query Language) is the standard language used to talk to a relational database - to create tables, insert data, search, update and delete. SQL is not case sensitive for keywords (SELECT = select), but writing keywords in UPPERCASE is a good habit. Every statement usually ends with a semicolon (;).

cards.title: Categories of SQL
cards.body: DDL (Data Definition Language): CREATE, ALTER, DROP, TRUNCATE. DML (Data Manipulation Language): INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE. DQL (Data Query Language): SELECT. DCL (Data Control Language): GRANT, REVOKE. TCL (Transaction Control Language): COMMIT, ROLLBACK, SAVEPOINT. This module focuses on DML, SELECT and joins.

quiz.question: Which statements belong to DML?
quiz.explanation: DML = INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE (SELECT is often grouped with it as DQL).

cards.title: Numeric Types
cards.body: INT - whole numbers. DECIMAL(10,2) - exact numbers with decimals (use for money). FLOAT / DOUBLE - approximate decimals. TINYINT(1) / BOOLEAN - true/false.

cards.title: Text Types
cards.body: CHAR(n) - fixed length text. VARCHAR(n) - variable length text up to n characters (names, emails). TEXT - long text such as descriptions.

cards.title: Date & Time Types
cards.body: DATE - 'YYYY-MM-DD'. TIME - 'HH:MM:SS'. DATETIME and TIMESTAMP - date and time together. YEAR - a four-digit year. Text and date values are written inside single quotes in SQL.

quiz.question: Which data type is best for a student's name?
quiz.explanation: VARCHAR stores variable length text such as names.

cards.title: CREATE DATABASE and USE
cards.body: CREATE DATABASE college; creates a new database. USE college; selects it so that following statements work inside it. SHOW DATABASES; lists all databases.

cards.title: CREATE TABLE
cards.body: CREATE TABLE departments (dept_id INT PRIMARY KEY, dept_name VARCHAR(50) NOT NULL); CREATE TABLE students (id INT PRIMARY KEY AUTO_INCREMENT, name VARCHAR(50) NOT NULL, city VARCHAR(30), dept_id INT, FOREIGN KEY (dept_id) REFERENCES departments(dept_id)); - AUTO_INCREMENT gives the next number automatically and NOT NULL forces a value.

cards.title: Constraints
cards.body: PRIMARY KEY, FOREIGN KEY, NOT NULL, UNIQUE, DEFAULT (default value) and CHECK (a condition) are constraints - rules that keep data correct.

quiz.question: Which statement selects the database 'college' for use?
quiz.explanation: USE database_name; makes it the current database.

modules.title: Connecting with MySQL Database
modules.description: Install MySQL, connect from the command line and connect from PHP and Java code.

cards.title: What is MySQL?
cards.body: MySQL is a free, open-source RDBMS. It works as a server that stores the databases and answers requests from clients. Popular with PHP, Java and Python web applications.

cards.title: Ways to Use MySQL
cards.body: Command-line client (mysql), MySQL Workbench (GUI), phpMyAdmin (web interface, comes with XAMPP/WAMP) and from program code. XAMPP is the easiest way for students: it installs Apache, MySQL and PHP together.

cards.title: Connection Details
cards.body: To connect you need 4 things: host (localhost or an IP), port (3306 by default), username (root for a local install) and password. The database name is chosen after connecting.

quiz.question: What is the default port of MySQL?
quiz.explanation: MySQL listens on port 3306 by default.

cards.title: Connect Command
cards.body: mysql -u root -p - then type the password. Full form: mysql -h localhost -P 3306 -u root -p. After connecting, the prompt changes to mysql>. Type exit or quit to leave.

cards.title: Useful Commands
cards.body: SHOW DATABASES; - list databases. USE college; - select a database. SHOW TABLES; - list tables. DESCRIBE students; (or DESC students;) - show the columns and data types of a table. SELECT DATABASE(); - show the current database.

cards.title: Running a Script
cards.body: Run an SQL file: mysql -u root -p college < data.sql. Inside the client use SOURCE data.sql; to execute a file.

quiz.question: Which command shows the structure (columns) of a table?
quiz.explanation: DESCRIBE (or DESC) lists the columns, types and keys of a table.

cards.title: MySQLi (Procedural)
cards.body: $conn = mysqli_connect("localhost", "root", "", "college"); - the four arguments are host, user, password and database. Always check: if (!$conn) { die("Connection failed: " . mysqli_connect_error()); }

cards.title: PDO
cards.body: PDO works with many databases: $pdo = new PDO("mysql:host=localhost;dbname=college;charset=utf8mb4", "root", ""); Set errors to exceptions: $pdo->setAttribute(PDO::ATTR_ERRMODE, PDO::ERRMODE_EXCEPTION);

cards.title: Closing
cards.body: Close the connection when done: mysqli_close($conn); (PDO closes when the object is destroyed: $pdo = null;).

quiz.question: In mysqli_connect(), what are the four arguments in order?
quiz.explanation: mysqli_connect(host, user, password, database).

cards.title: JDBC
cards.body: JDBC (Java Database Connectivity) is the Java API for databases. Add the MySQL Connector/J driver (a .jar file) to the project.

cards.title: Connection Code
cards.body: String url = "jdbc:mysql://localhost:3306/college"; Connection con = DriverManager.getConnection(url, "root", "password"); - the URL format is jdbc:mysql://host:port/database. Wrap it in try-catch for SQLException and close the connection with con.close() (or use try-with-resources).

quiz.question: Which URL format is correct for MySQL JDBC?
quiz.explanation: The JDBC URL is jdbc:mysql://host:port/database.

cards.title: Common Errors
cards.body: Access denied - wrong username or password. Unknown database - the database name is misspelled or not created. Can't connect to server - MySQL is not running or the port is wrong. Fix: start MySQL (XAMPP control panel), check host/port/credentials.

cards.title: Good Practice
cards.body: Do not use root in real applications - create a user with limited privileges. Never hard-code passwords in code that is shared; keep them in a config file outside the public folder. Always close connections.

quiz.question: What does the error 'Access denied for user' usually mean?
quiz.explanation: It means the credentials (or privileges) are wrong.

modules.title: Basic Database Operations (DML)
modules.description: INSERT, SELECT with filters, UPDATE, DELETE, query parameters and executing queries.

cards.title: Basic INSERT
cards.body: INSERT INTO departments (dept_id, dept_name) VALUES (10, 'Computer'); - lists the columns, then the values in the same order. Text and dates go inside single quotes; numbers do not.

cards.title: Insert Several Rows
cards.body: INSERT INTO students (name, city, dept_id) VALUES ('Rahul', 'Guwahati', 10), ('Rani', 'Delhi', 20), ('Sumit', 'Guwahati', 10); - one statement can add many rows. The id is skipped because it is AUTO_INCREMENT.

cards.title: Insert Notes
cards.body: If you skip a column it gets its DEFAULT value or NULL. A column that is NOT NULL with no default must be given a value. Inserting a duplicate primary key or an unknown foreign key gives an error. INSERT INTO ... SELECT copies rows from another table.

quiz.question: Which statement adds a new row to a table?
quiz.explanation: INSERT INTO table (columns) VALUES (values); adds a row.

cards.title: Basic SELECT
cards.body: SELECT * FROM students; - all columns, all rows. SELECT name, city FROM students; - only the chosen columns. The * means 'all columns' (list columns explicitly in real projects).

cards.title: Aliases
cards.body: AS gives a column or table a temporary name: SELECT name AS student_name FROM students AS s; Aliases make results and joins easier to read.

cards.title: Order of a SELECT
cards.body: SELECT columns FROM table WHERE condition GROUP BY column HAVING condition ORDER BY column LIMIT n; - the clauses are written in this order.

quiz.question: Which query returns only the name and city columns?
quiz.explanation: List the wanted columns after SELECT.

cards.title: WHERE
cards.body: WHERE filters rows: SELECT * FROM students WHERE city = 'Guwahati'; Only rows where the condition is true are returned.

cards.title: Comparison & Logical Operators
cards.body: =, <> (or !=), <, >, <=, >=. Combine with AND (both true), OR (either true) and NOT. Example: WHERE city = 'Delhi' OR dept_id = 10. Use parentheses when mixing AND and OR.

cards.title: Special Operators
cards.body: BETWEEN 10 AND 20 - within a range (inclusive). IN ('Delhi','Pune') - matches any value in a list. LIKE 'R%' - pattern: % = any characters, _ = exactly one character. IS NULL / IS NOT NULL - test for missing values (never use = NULL).

quiz.question: How do you find rows where dept_id has no value?
quiz.explanation: NULL must be tested with IS NULL; = NULL never matches.

cards.title: ORDER BY
cards.body: Sorts the result: SELECT * FROM students ORDER BY name ASC; (ascending is the default) or DESC for descending. You can sort by several columns: ORDER BY city, name DESC.

cards.title: LIMIT
cards.body: LIMIT 5 returns only the first 5 rows. LIMIT 10, 5 (or LIMIT 5 OFFSET 10) skips 10 rows and returns the next 5 - used for pagination.

cards.title: DISTINCT
cards.body: SELECT DISTINCT city FROM students; removes duplicate values from the result.

quiz.question: Which keyword removes duplicate rows from a result?
quiz.explanation: SELECT DISTINCT returns each different value only once.

cards.title: Aggregate Functions
cards.body: COUNT() - number of rows. SUM() - total. AVG() - average. MIN() / MAX() - smallest / largest. Example: SELECT COUNT(*) FROM students;

cards.title: GROUP BY
cards.body: Groups rows with the same value so you can summarise each group: SELECT city, COUNT(*) FROM students GROUP BY city;

cards.title: HAVING
cards.body: HAVING filters groups after grouping (WHERE filters rows before grouping): SELECT city, COUNT(*) AS total FROM students GROUP BY city HAVING total > 1;

quiz.question: Which clause filters groups created by GROUP BY?
quiz.explanation: HAVING filters groups; WHERE filters individual rows.

cards.title: UPDATE Syntax
cards.body: UPDATE students SET city = 'Mumbai' WHERE id = 4; - SET gives the new value, WHERE selects which rows. Several columns: SET city = 'Mumbai', dept_id = 20.

cards.title: Danger: Missing WHERE
cards.body: Without WHERE, every row in the table is updated! Always write the WHERE clause first, and test it with a SELECT using the same condition before running UPDATE.

cards.title: Check the Result
cards.body: After UPDATE, MySQL reports the number of rows matched and changed. Zero rows means the WHERE condition matched nothing.

quiz.question: What happens if UPDATE has no WHERE clause?
options: Only the first row is updated
quiz.explanation: Without WHERE, UPDATE changes every row of the table.

cards.title: DELETE Syntax
cards.body: DELETE FROM students WHERE id = 4; removes the matching rows. Without WHERE, DELETE FROM students; removes all rows (the table structure remains).

cards.title: DELETE vs TRUNCATE vs DROP
cards.body: DELETE - removes selected rows, can use WHERE, can be rolled back inside a transaction. TRUNCATE TABLE - removes all rows quickly and resets AUTO_INCREMENT. DROP TABLE - removes the whole table (structure and data).

cards.title: Foreign Key Rule
cards.body: You cannot delete a parent row (a department) while child rows (students) still refer to it, unless the foreign key uses ON DELETE CASCADE. Delete the children first or use CASCADE carefully.

quiz.question: Which statement removes the whole table including its structure?
quiz.explanation: DROP TABLE deletes structure and data; DELETE and TRUNCATE keep the structure.

cards.title: Why Parameters?
cards.body: Programs often need values typed by users: SELECT * FROM students WHERE city = ?. Building the query by joining strings ("... WHERE city = '" + city + "'") is dangerous because of SQL injection - a user could type SQL code as the value. Parameters keep data and SQL separate.

cards.title: Prepared Statement in PHP (mysqli)
cards.body: $stmt = $conn->prepare("SELECT * FROM students WHERE city = ? AND dept_id = ?"); $stmt->bind_param("si", $city, $dept); - the ? are placeholders; "si" means string then integer. Types: s = string, i = integer, d = double, b = blob. Then $stmt->execute();

cards.title: Prepared Statement in PDO and Java
cards.body: PDO: $stmt = $pdo->prepare("SELECT * FROM students WHERE city = :city"); $stmt->execute([':city' => $city]); Java: PreparedStatement ps = con.prepareStatement("SELECT * FROM students WHERE city = ?"); ps.setString(1, city); - parameter numbers start at 1.

quiz.question: What is the main security benefit of query parameters (prepared statements)?
quiz.explanation: Placeholders keep user input as data, so it cannot change the SQL command.

cards.title: Execute in PHP
cards.body: $result = mysqli_query($conn, "SELECT * FROM students"); while ($row = mysqli_fetch_assoc($result)) { echo $row['name']; } - fetch_assoc returns one row at a time as an array. mysqli_num_rows($result) gives the number of rows. For INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE, mysqli_query returns true/false and mysqli_affected_rows($conn) gives the changed rows.

cards.title: Execute in Java
cards.body: Statement st = con.createStatement(); ResultSet rs = st.executeQuery("SELECT * FROM students"); while (rs.next()) { System.out.println(rs.getString("name")); } - use executeQuery() for SELECT and executeUpdate() for INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE (returns the number of affected rows).

cards.title: Handle Errors
cards.body: Always check if the query succeeded: mysqli_error($conn) in PHP or catch SQLException in Java. Free the result and close the connection when finished.

quiz.question: In JDBC, which method runs an INSERT, UPDATE or DELETE?
quiz.explanation: executeUpdate() is for DML that changes data; executeQuery() is for SELECT.

modules.title: SQL Joins
modules.description: Combine data from several tables with cross, inner, outer and self joins.

cards.title: Purpose of a Join
cards.body: Related data is spread over several tables. A JOIN combines rows from two or more tables using a related column (usually primary key = foreign key). It lets you show a student's name together with the department name.

cards.title: Sample Data for the Next Lessons
cards.body: departments: (10, Computer), (20, Commerce), (30, Arts). students: (1, Rahul, 10), (2, Rani, 20), (3, Sumit, 10), (4, Anita, NULL). Note: Anita has no department and Arts has no students - useful for seeing the difference between join types.

cards.title: Types of Joins
cards.body: CROSS JOIN, INNER JOIN, OUTER JOINS (LEFT, RIGHT, FULL) and SELF JOIN.

quiz.question: What does a JOIN do?
options: Combines rows from two or more tables
quiz.explanation: A join combines rows from multiple tables using a related column.

cards.title: What is a Cross Join?
cards.body: A cross join (Cartesian product) pairs every row of the first table with every row of the second table. No condition is used. SELECT s.name, d.dept_name FROM students s CROSS JOIN departments d;

cards.title: Result Size
cards.body: Rows in result = rows in table 1 x rows in table 2. With 4 students and 3 departments the result has 12 rows. It grows very fast, so use it only when you really need all combinations (e.g. every size with every colour). Forgetting the join condition in a normal join accidentally makes a cross join.

quiz.question: 4 students CROSS JOIN 3 departments gives how many rows?
quiz.explanation: A cross join returns rows1 x rows2 = 4 x 3 = 12.

cards.title: What is an Inner Join?
cards.body: An inner join returns only the rows that have a match in both tables. SELECT s.name, d.dept_name FROM students s INNER JOIN departments d ON s.dept_id = d.dept_id; JOIN alone means INNER JOIN.

cards.title: Result
cards.body: With the sample data you get Rahul-Computer, Rani-Commerce and Sumit-Computer (3 rows). Anita is missing (no dept_id) and Arts is missing (no students).

cards.title: ON vs WHERE
cards.body: ON gives the joining condition; WHERE filters the joined result afterwards, e.g. ... ON s.dept_id = d.dept_id WHERE d.dept_name = 'Computer'.

quiz.question: Which rows does an INNER JOIN return?
options: Only rows with a match in both tables
All rows of the left table
quiz.explanation: Inner join keeps only matching rows from both tables.

cards.title: LEFT JOIN
cards.body: A left (outer) join returns all rows of the left table and the matching rows of the right table. When there is no match, the right side columns are NULL. SELECT s.name, d.dept_name FROM students s LEFT JOIN departments d ON s.dept_id = d.dept_id;

cards.title: Result
cards.body: Rahul-Computer, Rani-Commerce, Sumit-Computer and Anita-NULL (4 rows). Every student appears, even Anita.

cards.title: Find Unmatched Rows
cards.body: Add WHERE d.dept_id IS NULL to list students who have no department.

quiz.question: In a LEFT JOIN, unmatched rows from the right table show...
quiz.explanation: Left join keeps all left rows; missing right-side values are NULL.

cards.title: RIGHT JOIN
cards.body: A right (outer) join returns all rows of the right table and the matching rows of the left table; missing left side values are NULL. SELECT s.name, d.dept_name FROM students s RIGHT JOIN departments d ON s.dept_id = d.dept_id;

cards.title: Result
cards.body: Rahul-Computer, Sumit-Computer, Rani-Commerce and NULL-Arts (4 rows). Arts appears although it has no students.

cards.title: Tip
cards.body: A RIGHT JOIN can always be written as a LEFT JOIN by swapping the table order, so many developers use only LEFT JOIN.

quiz.question: Which join keeps all rows of the right table?
quiz.explanation: RIGHT JOIN keeps every row of the right table.

cards.title: FULL OUTER JOIN
cards.body: A full outer join returns all rows from both tables, matched where possible and NULL where not. Result: Rahul-Computer, Rani-Commerce, Sumit-Computer, Anita-NULL and NULL-Arts.

cards.title: In MySQL
cards.body: MySQL does not support FULL OUTER JOIN directly. Combine a LEFT JOIN and a RIGHT JOIN with UNION: SELECT s.name, d.dept_name FROM students s LEFT JOIN departments d ON s.dept_id = d.dept_id UNION SELECT s.name, d.dept_name FROM students s RIGHT JOIN departments d ON s.dept_id = d.dept_id; (UNION removes duplicates.)

quiz.question: How can you do a FULL OUTER JOIN in MySQL?
quiz.explanation: MySQL lacks FULL OUTER JOIN; combine LEFT and RIGHT joins with UNION.

cards.title: What is a Self Join?
cards.body: A self join joins a table with itself. You must give the table two different aliases so MySQL can tell the copies apart. It is used for hierarchies in one table, such as employees and their managers.

cards.title: Example
cards.body: employees(emp_id, name, manager_id): (1, Meena, NULL), (2, Ravi, 1), (3, Anil, 1). SELECT e.name AS employee, m.name AS manager FROM employees e JOIN employees m ON e.manager_id = m.emp_id; Result: Ravi-Meena, Anil-Meena. Use LEFT JOIN to also show Meena who has no manager.

cards.title: Other Uses
cards.body: Finding pairs in the same city, or duplicate values: SELECT a.name, b.name FROM students a JOIN students b ON a.city = b.city AND a.id < b.id;

quiz.question: What is required to write a self join?
options: Different aliases for the same table
A foreign key to another table
quiz.explanation: The same table is used twice, so each copy needs its own alias.

cards.title: Quick Comparison
cards.body: INNER - only matching rows. LEFT - all left + matches. RIGHT - all right + matches. FULL - all rows of both (UNION in MySQL). CROSS - every combination. SELF - table joined with itself.

cards.title: Joining Three Tables
cards.body: Add another JOIN: SELECT s.name, c.course_name FROM students s JOIN enrollments e ON s.id = e.student_id JOIN courses c ON e.course_id = c.course_id; - this is how many-to-many relationships are read through a linking table.

cards.title: Good Habits
cards.body: Use table aliases, qualify columns (s.name), always write the ON condition and join on indexed key columns for speed. Combine joins with WHERE, ORDER BY and GROUP BY, e.g. count students per department: SELECT d.dept_name, COUNT(s.id) FROM departments d LEFT JOIN students s ON d.dept_id = s.dept_id GROUP BY d.dept_name;

quiz.question: Which join shows ALL departments even those with zero students?
quiz.explanation: A LEFT JOIN from departments keeps every department, with NULL/0 for those without students.

units.title: Module 9: AJAX & jQuery
units.description: Asynchronous web development: AJAX with XMLHttpRequest, Fetch and async/await, the jQuery library (selectors, DOM, events, effects, AJAX), and using them with Django.

modules.title: Introduction to AJAX
modules.description: What AJAX is, how a request travels from browser to server and back, and the HTTP, data-format and security basics you need before writing code.

cards.title: Definition & Purpose
cards.body: AJAX stands for Asynchronous JavaScript And XML. It is not a language or a library but a technique: JavaScript sends a request to the server in the background and updates only part of the page with the response, without a full page reload. Examples: Gmail loading new mail, Google Maps loading tiles as you drag, live search suggestions, like buttons, and form validation while you type.

cards.title: How AJAX Works (Part 1)
cards.body: 1) An event happens (button click, key press, page load). 2) JavaScript creates a request using XMLHttpRequest, fetch() or jQuery. 3) The browser sends it to the server in the background.

cards.title: How AJAX Works (Part 2)
cards.body: 4) The server processes it (database, logic) and returns data, usually JSON. 5) A JavaScript callback receives the response. 6) JavaScript updates the DOM, changing just the needed part of the page. The user can keep working throughout.

cards.title: Benefits & Limitations
cards.body: Benefits: faster, smoother experience, less bandwidth (only needed data travels), reduced server load, and desktop-like interactivity. Limitations: needs JavaScript enabled, the Back button and bookmarks do not track dynamic changes unless you use the History API, content loaded dynamically is harder for some search engines, and debugging asynchronous code is harder.

quiz.question: What does AJAX allow a web page to do?
options: Exchange data with the server and update part of the page without reloading
quiz.explanation: AJAX sends requests in the background and updates only part of the page, so the full page does not reload.

cards.title: Synchronous (Blocking)
cards.body: In a synchronous request the browser waits for the server's reply before running the next line of code, so the page freezes while waiting. Traditional form submissions and links work this way: each action loads a whole new page. Synchronous XMLHttpRequest on the main thread is deprecated because it hurts user experience.

cards.title: Asynchronous (Non-blocking)
cards.body: An asynchronous request is sent and JavaScript continues running immediately; the reply is handled later by a callback, promise or async/await continuation. JavaScript is single-threaded, but the browser's event loop lets slow operations (network, timers) finish in the background and then queues their callbacks to run. This is why the page stays responsive during an AJAX call.

quiz.question: What is the main feature of an asynchronous request?
options: The page freezes until the server replies
The script continues running while waiting for the response
It works only for POST requests
quiz.explanation: Asynchronous requests do not block: code continues to run and the response is handled later via a callback or promise.

cards.title: JSON
cards.body: JSON (JavaScript Object Notation) is the standard AJAX data format: lightweight, readable, and natively supported by JavaScript. Example: '{"id": 1, "name": "Asha", "skills": ["Python", "JS"]}'. Keys must be in double quotes. 'JSON.parse(text)' converts a JSON string to an object, and 'JSON.stringify(obj)' converts an object to a JSON string. Servers label it with 'Content-Type: application/json'.

cards.title: XML, HTML Fragments & Plain Text (Part 1)
cards.body: XML (the 'X' in AJAX) uses custom tags such as '<student><name>Asha</name></student>' and needs parsing with DOMParser or responseXML; it is verbose, so it is rarely used for new APIs.

cards.title: XML, HTML Fragments & Plain Text (Part 2)
cards.body: A server can also return an HTML fragment that you insert directly into the page (the approach behind jQuery's load() and Django template partials), or plain text. Choose JSON for data and HTML fragments for ready-made markup.

quiz.question: Which JavaScript method converts a JSON string into a JavaScript object?
quiz.explanation: JSON.parse() turns a JSON string into an object; JSON.stringify() does the reverse.

lessons.title: HTTP Basics, CORS & Security for AJAX

cards.title: HTTP Methods & Status Codes (Part 1)
cards.body: GET retrieves data (parameters in the URL, can be cached, never changes data), POST creates data (sent in the body), PUT replaces and PATCH partially updates a resource, DELETE removes it.

cards.title: HTTP Methods & Status Codes (Part 2)
cards.body: Status codes: 200 OK, 201 Created, 204 No Content, 301/302 redirects, 400 Bad Request, 401 Unauthorized, 403 Forbidden, 404 Not Found, 500 Internal Server Error. Headers carry metadata such as Content-Type, Accept and Authorization.

cards.title: Same-Origin Policy & CORS (Part 1)
cards.body: Browsers only let a script read responses from the same origin (same scheme, host and port) as the page. To call another origin, the server must opt in with CORS headers such as 'Access-Control-Allow-Origin'.

cards.title: Same-Origin Policy & CORS (Part 2)
cards.body: For requests that are not 'simple' (for example JSON POST or custom headers) the browser first sends an OPTIONS preflight request. A 'CORS error' in the console means the server did not allow your origin.

cards.title: CSRF & XSS Basics (Part 1)
cards.body: CSRF (Cross-Site Request Forgery): a malicious site tricks a logged-in user's browser into sending a request; frameworks like Django require a CSRF token on POST/PUT/DELETE, which AJAX must send in the 'X-CSRFToken' header.

cards.title: CSRF & XSS Basics (Part 2)
cards.body: XSS (Cross-Site Scripting): injecting scripts through untrusted data; never insert user-supplied text as HTML (use textContent or jQuery's .text()). Always validate on the server too; client-side checks are only for convenience.

quiz.question: Two URLs have the same origin only if they share which three things?
quiz.explanation: An origin is the combination of scheme (http/https), host and port. Different path or query does not change the origin.

modules.title: AJAX with XMLHttpRequest
modules.description: The original browser API for AJAX: creating requests, tracking readyState, sending GET and POST data, and handling responses and errors.

cards.title: Creating & Sending a Request
cards.body: Steps: 'var xhr = new XMLHttpRequest();' then 'xhr.open("GET", "data.json", true);' (method, URL, async flag), set up the handler, then 'xhr.send();'. The third argument true means asynchronous. Despite the name, XMLHttpRequest can fetch JSON, HTML or plain text, not just XML.

cards.title: readyState & status
cards.body: 'xhr.readyState' goes through 0 UNSENT, 1 OPENED, 2 HEADERS_RECEIVED, 3 LOADING and 4 DONE. 'xhr.onreadystatechange = function() { if (xhr.readyState === 4 && xhr.status === 200) { ... } }' is the classic pattern. 'xhr.status' is the HTTP code (200, 404...) and 'xhr.statusText' its text. The modern shortcut is 'xhr.onload', which fires when the request completes.

cards.title: Reading the Response
cards.body: 'xhr.responseText' holds the response as a string, 'xhr.responseXML' as an XML document, and 'xhr.response' depends on 'xhr.responseType' (set 'json' to get a parsed object directly). Typical use: 'document.getElementById("result").innerHTML = xhr.responseText;' or 'var data = JSON.parse(xhr.responseText);' followed by DOM updates.

quiz.question: Which readyState value means the request is complete and the response is ready?
quiz.explanation: readyState 4 (DONE) means the operation is complete. Check status === 200 to confirm success.

cards.title: GET with Parameters
cards.body: For GET, send data in the query string, and encode values: 'xhr.open("GET", "search?q=" + encodeURIComponent(term), true); xhr.send();'. 'encodeURIComponent' safely escapes spaces and symbols such as '&' and '='. GET is for reading data only and can be cached by the browser; add a changing parameter if you need fresh data every time.

cards.title: POST with Form Data
cards.body: POST sends data in the request body: 'xhr.open("POST", "save", true); xhr.setRequestHeader("Content-Type", "application/x-www-form-urlencoded"); xhr.send("name=Asha&age=21");'. Call setRequestHeader after open() and before send(). With a form element, 'new FormData(formElement)' builds multipart data (including files) and the browser sets the Content-Type for you.

cards.title: Sending JSON
cards.body: To send JSON, set the header and stringify the data: 'xhr.setRequestHeader("Content-Type", "application/json"); xhr.send(JSON.stringify({name: "Asha", age: 21}));'. The server must read the request body and parse it as JSON (in Django: 'json.loads(request.body)'). Remember to include the CSRF header for frameworks that require it.

quiz.question: Which method must be called after open() and before send() to set a request header?
quiz.explanation: setRequestHeader(name, value) must be called between open() and send().

cards.title: Checking Success & Failure
cards.body: A completed request is not always a successful one: a 404 or 500 still ends with readyState 4. Always check 'xhr.status' (200-299 is success). 'xhr.onerror' fires on network failure (offline, DNS, CORS block), while HTTP errors arrive through onload with a bad status. Show the user a friendly message and consider a retry option.

cards.title: Timeout, Abort & Progress
cards.body: 'xhr.timeout = 5000' sets a limit in milliseconds and 'xhr.ontimeout' handles expiry. 'xhr.abort()' cancels an in-flight request, useful when a newer search replaces an older one. 'xhr.onprogress' and 'xhr.upload.onprogress' report bytes loaded, which lets you build progress bars for downloads and uploads.

quiz.question: Which event fires when a network failure (such as being offline) prevents the request?
quiz.explanation: onerror handles network-level failures. HTTP error codes such as 404 still arrive through onload with the status set.

modules.title: Modern AJAX: Promises, Fetch & async/await
modules.description: Cleaner asynchronous code with promises, the Fetch API and async/await, plus the AJAX patterns used in real applications.

cards.title: Callbacks & Callback Hell
cards.body: A callback is a function passed to another function to run later, e.g. 'setTimeout(fn, 1000)' or an XHR onload handler. When several asynchronous steps depend on each other (get user, then get orders, then get items), callbacks nest deeper and deeper, producing hard-to-read 'callback hell' with scattered error handling. Promises solve this.

cards.title: Promises
cards.body: A Promise represents a value that will arrive later and is in one of three states: pending, fulfilled (resolved) or rejected. Create one with 'new Promise((resolve, reject) => { ... })'. Consume it with '.then(onSuccess)', '.catch(onError)' and '.finally(cleanup)'. '.then()' calls can be chained because each returns a new promise, flattening nested callbacks.

cards.title: Combining Promises
cards.body: 'Promise.all([p1, p2, p3])' waits for all of them and rejects if any fails (good for loading independent data in parallel). 'Promise.allSettled()' waits for all regardless of failure, 'Promise.race()' resolves with the first to settle, and 'Promise.any()' with the first to succeed.

quiz.question: Which are the three states of a JavaScript Promise?
quiz.explanation: A promise starts pending and ends either fulfilled (success) or rejected (failure).

cards.title: Basic fetch()
cards.body: 'fetch(url)' returns a promise for a Response object and is the modern replacement for XMLHttpRequest. Pattern: 'fetch("/api/students").then(res => res.json()).then(data => console.log(data)).catch(err => console.error(err));'. Body readers: res.json(), res.text(), res.blob(), res.formData(); each returns another promise.

cards.title: Checking Errors Correctly
cards.body: Important: fetch rejects its promise only on network failure. A 404 or 500 still resolves, so check 'res.ok' (true for 200-299) or 'res.status': 'fetch(url).then(res => { if (!res.ok) throw new Error("HTTP " + res.status); return res.json(); })'. Without this check, error pages may be parsed as data and fail strangely.

cards.title: POST & Options
cards.body: Second argument configures the request: 'fetch("/api/save", { method: "POST", headers: {"Content-Type": "application/json", "X-CSRFToken": token}, body: JSON.stringify(data) })'. Other options: 'credentials: "include"' (send cookies cross-origin), 'cache', 'mode', and 'signal' for cancellation. Default method is GET.

quiz.question: A fetch() call receives a 404 response from the server. What happens to the promise?
options: It resolves; you must check response.ok
quiz.explanation: fetch only rejects on network errors. HTTP error statuses resolve normally, so you check res.ok or res.status yourself.

cards.title: async and await
cards.body: 'async' before a function makes it return a promise, and 'await' pauses inside it until a promise settles, so asynchronous code reads like synchronous code: 'async function load() { const res = await fetch(url); const data = await res.json(); show(data); }'. Await only works inside async functions (or top-level modules). The rest of the page keeps running while it waits.

cards.title: Error Handling with try/catch
cards.body: Wrap awaits in try/catch/finally: 'try { const res = await fetch(url); if (!res.ok) throw new Error(res.status); const data = await res.json(); } catch (e) { showError(e.message); } finally { hideSpinner(); }'. Run independent calls in parallel with 'const [a, b] = await Promise.all([fetch(u1), fetch(u2)]);' instead of awaiting them one after another.

cards.title: Cancelling Requests
cards.body: Use AbortController: 'const ctrl = new AbortController(); fetch(url, { signal: ctrl.signal }); ctrl.abort();'. The promise rejects with an AbortError, which you can ignore. This prevents stale responses from overwriting newer ones, for example in live search when the user keeps typing.

quiz.question: Where can the await keyword be used?
quiz.explanation: await is valid inside async functions (and at the top level of ES modules).

cards.title: Form Submit Without Reload
cards.body: Intercept the submit event, stop the default navigation, and send the data: 'form.addEventListener("submit", async e => { e.preventDefault(); const res = await fetch(form.action, { method: "POST", body: new FormData(form) }); ... });'. Show a spinner, disable the button to prevent double submission, and display validation errors returned by the server.

cards.title: Live Search & Debounce
cards.body: Sending a request on every keystroke wastes bandwidth. Debounce: wait until the user pauses (for example 300 ms) before sending, using 'clearTimeout(timer); timer = setTimeout(search, 300);'. Combine it with AbortController so only the latest query's response is displayed. Requires at least 2-3 characters before searching.

cards.title: Polling, Load More & Infinite Scroll
cards.body: Polling: 'setInterval(fetchStatus, 5000)' repeatedly asks the server for updates (use WebSockets or Server-Sent Events for true real time). Load More: a button requests the next page ('?page=2') and appends the results. Infinite scroll: an IntersectionObserver or scroll event triggers the next page when the user nears the bottom.

quiz.question: What is the purpose of debouncing in a live-search box?
options: To avoid sending a request on every keystroke
quiz.explanation: Debouncing waits until typing pauses, so far fewer requests are sent to the server.

modules.title: Introduction to jQuery
modules.description: Setting up jQuery, selecting elements, reading and changing content, styling, and traversing the DOM.

cards.title: Overview
cards.body: jQuery is a fast, small JavaScript library with the motto 'write less, do more'. It simplifies selecting elements, handling events, DOM changes, animations and AJAX, and smooths over old browser differences. Today vanilla JavaScript can do most of this, but jQuery is still widely used in older code bases, Bootstrap 4 and the Django admin, so you need to read and write it.

cards.title: Adding jQuery to a Page
cards.body: Use a CDN: '<script src="https://code.jquery.com/jquery-3.7.1.min.js"></script>' placed before your own script, or download the file and reference it locally (in Django, via the static folder). The 'slim' build omits the AJAX and effects modules, so use the full build for this course. If another library already uses the $ symbol, call 'jQuery.noConflict()'.

cards.title: Basic Syntax & Document Ready
cards.body: Syntax: '$(selector).action()'. '$' (an alias of 'jQuery') selects elements, and the action is performed on them. Wait for the DOM to be ready: '$(document).ready(function() { ... });' or the shorthand '$(function() { ... });'. This prevents code from running before the elements exist. jQuery methods usually return the jQuery object, which enables chaining: '$("#box").addClass("on").fadeIn();'.

quiz.question: What is the correct jQuery shorthand for the document ready handler?
quiz.explanation: $(function(){...}) is shorthand for $(document).ready(function(){...}).

cards.title: Basic Selectors
cards.body: '$("p")' selects by tag, '$("#id")' by id, '$(".class")' by class, '$("*")' everything, '$("h1, h2, p")' a group, and '$(this)' the current element inside an event handler. Selectors use CSS syntax, so any valid CSS selector works. The result is a jQuery object that may contain zero, one or many elements; check 'length' to see how many matched.

cards.title: Hierarchy & Attribute Selectors
cards.body: '$("div p")' descendant, '$("div > p")' direct child, '$("h2 + p")' immediately following sibling, '$("h2 ~ p")' all following siblings. Attributes: '$("[href]")' has attribute, '$("input[type=text]")' equals value, '$("a[href^=https]")' starts with, '$("a[href$=pdf]")' ends with, '$("a[href*=shop]")' contains.

cards.title: jQuery Filters & Form Selectors
cards.body: Positional filters: ':first', ':last', ':even', ':odd', ':eq(n)', ':gt(n)', ':lt(n)'. Content/visibility: ':contains(text)', ':empty', ':visible', ':hidden'. Form helpers: ':input', ':text', ':password', ':checkbox', ':checked', ':selected', ':disabled'. Example: '$("tr:even").css("background", "#eee")' stripes a table. Note that :even and :odd are zero-indexed.

quiz.question: Which selector picks all direct child paragraphs of a div?
quiz.explanation: The > combinator selects direct children only; the space selects all descendants.

cards.title: text(), html() and val()
cards.body: Called with no argument they get; with an argument they set. 'text()' reads or sets plain text (safe), 'html()' reads or sets HTML markup, and 'val()' reads or sets the value of form fields. Examples: '$("#msg").text("Saved!")', '$("#box").html("Hi")', 'var name = $("#name").val();'. Prefer text() when inserting user-provided data to avoid XSS.

cards.title: attr(), prop() and data()
cards.body: 'attr(name)' / 'attr(name, value)' work with HTML attributes such as href, src and id; 'removeAttr(name)' deletes one. 'prop()' reads or sets live properties, which is the right choice for checkboxes and dropdowns: '$("#agree").prop("checked")' returns true or false. 'data("id")' reads a 'data-id' attribute (with automatic type conversion).

cards.title: Callbacks in Setters
cards.body: Setters accept a function that receives the index and old value and returns the new value: '$("li").text(function(i, old) { return (i + 1) + ". " + old; });'. This applies the change to every matched element individually and is cleaner than writing a loop.

quiz.question: Which method should you use to check whether a checkbox is checked?
quiz.explanation: prop("checked") reflects the current state as true/false, whereas the checked attribute only reflects the initial HTML.

cards.title: Adding Elements
cards.body:
'append()' inserts content at the end inside the selected element, 'prepend()' at the start, 'after()' and 'before()' insert outside it as siblings. Reverse forms 'appendTo()' and 'prependTo()' flip target and content. Example: '$("ul").append("
  • New item
    • ")'. Create elements with '$("
  • ").text("Item").addClass("x")'. 'clone()' duplicates elements.

cards.title: Removing Elements
cards.body: 'remove()' deletes the element (and its data and events) from the DOM, 'empty()' deletes only its children, and 'detach()' removes it but keeps data and events so you can reinsert it later. 'remove(".old")' can take a filter selector. Use 'replaceWith()' to swap content and 'wrap()' to surround elements with another.

cards.title: CSS Classes & Styles
cards.body: 'addClass()', 'removeClass()', 'toggleClass()' and 'hasClass()' manage classes, which is the preferred way to style (keep CSS in stylesheets). 'css("color", "red")' sets one property, 'css({color: "red", fontSize: "20px"})' sets several, and 'css("color")' reads a computed value.

cards.title: Dimensions & Position
cards.body: 'width()' and 'height()' give content size; 'innerWidth()' adds padding, 'outerWidth()' adds padding and border ('outerWidth(true)' adds margin). 'offset()' returns an element's position relative to the document, 'position()' relative to its offset parent, and 'scrollTop()' gets or sets vertical scroll. Calling '$(window).width()' returns the viewport width.

quiz.question: Which method removes an element but keeps its data and event handlers so it can be re-inserted later?
quiz.explanation: detach() removes the element from the DOM while preserving data and events. remove() discards them.

cards.title: Moving Through the DOM
cards.body: Up: 'parent()', 'parents()', 'closest(selector)' (nearest matching ancestor, very useful in event handlers). Down: 'children()' (direct), 'find(selector)' (any depth). Sideways: 'siblings()', 'next()', 'prev()', 'nextAll()', 'prevAll()'. Example: '$(this).closest("tr").find(".price").text()' finds the price cell in the same table row as a clicked button.

cards.title: Narrowing Selections
cards.body: 'first()', 'last()', 'eq(n)' pick by position; 'filter(selector or fn)' keeps matches; 'not(selector)' excludes; 'has(selector)' keeps elements containing a match; 'is(selector)' returns true or false. Because every method returns a jQuery object, steps chain into readable pipelines.

cards.title: each() and Chaining (Part 1)
cards.body: '$("li").each(function(index, el) { ... })' loops over matched elements ('this' is the DOM element, return false to break). '$.each(array_or_object, function(key, value) { ... })' loops over data.

cards.title: each() and Chaining (Part 2)
cards.body: Chaining runs several actions on one selection without re-selecting: '$("#box").css("color", "red").slideUp(300).slideDown(300);'. Store selections in variables if you reuse them, to avoid repeated DOM searches.

quiz.question: Which traversal method returns the nearest ancestor that matches a selector?
quiz.explanation: closest() starts at the element itself and walks up the tree until it finds a match.

modules.title: jQuery Events & Effects
modules.description: Responding to user actions, delegating events, and creating show/hide, fade, slide and custom animations.

cards.title: Common Events & on() (Part 1)
cards.body: Mouse: click, dblclick, mouseenter, mouseleave, hover(in, out). Keyboard: keydown, keyup. Form: submit, change, focus, blur, input. Window: ready, resize, scroll. Attach handlers with 'on()': '$("#btn").on("click", function() { alert("Hi"); });'.

cards.title: Common Events & on() (Part 2)
cards.body: Multiple events: 'on("mouseenter mouseleave", fn)'. Remove with 'off()', and run once with 'one()'. Shorthands like '.click(fn)' still work, but 'on()' is the recommended form.

cards.title: The Event Object
cards.body: The handler receives an event object: 'e.target' (the element that triggered it), 'e.type', 'e.key' or 'e.which' (keyboard), 'e.pageX/pageY' (mouse). Control the flow with 'e.preventDefault()' (stop the default action such as a link or form submit) and 'e.stopPropagation()' (stop bubbling to parent elements). Inside the handler, 'this' is the DOM element and '$(this)' wraps it for jQuery methods.

cards.title: Event Delegation
cards.body: Handlers attached directly only affect elements that exist at that moment. For dynamic content (rows added by AJAX) delegate from a stable parent: '$("#list").on("click", ".delete", function() { $(this).closest("li").remove(); });'. The event bubbles up to #list, and jQuery checks whether the target matches '.delete'. This also uses one handler instead of hundreds.

quiz.question: Elements are added to a list dynamically by AJAX. How do you make clicks on their '.delete' buttons work?
options: Attach click handlers once at page load directly to .delete
Reload the page after every addition
quiz.explanation: Delegating to a stable parent handles clicks for elements that are added later, because events bubble up to the parent.

cards.title: Show, Hide & Toggle
cards.body: 'show()', 'hide()' and 'toggle()' change visibility, optionally animated with a speed: 'slow' (600 ms), 'fast' (200 ms) or milliseconds, plus a callback that runs when finished: '$("#box").hide(500, function() { console.log("done"); });'. hide() sets 'display: none', so the element takes no space.

cards.title: Fade & Slide
cards.body: Fading changes opacity: 'fadeIn()', 'fadeOut()', 'fadeToggle()', and 'fadeTo(speed, opacity)' to a specific level. Sliding changes height: 'slideDown()', 'slideUp()', 'slideToggle()', commonly used for accordions and dropdown menus. Example: '$(".panel").slideToggle(300);' on a heading click.

cards.title: Controlling Effects
cards.body: 'delay(ms)' pauses the queue between effects, 'stop()' halts the current animation (use it to prevent a build-up of queued animations from repeated hovering: '$(el).stop().fadeIn()'), and 'finish()' jumps to the end of all queued animations. Callback functions guarantee the next step runs only after the effect completes.

quiz.question: Which jQuery method fades an element to a specific opacity level?
quiz.explanation: fadeTo(speed, opacity) animates the opacity to the value you provide, e.g. 0.5.

cards.title: animate() Basics (Part 1)
cards.body: '$(selector).animate({properties}, duration, easing, callback)'. Example: '$("#box").animate({left: "250px", opacity: 0.5, height: "+=50px"}, 1000);'. Only numeric CSS properties can be animated (width, height, left, opacity, fontSize...).

cards.title: animate() Basics (Part 2)
cards.body: Prefix a value with '+=' or '-=' for relative changes. To animate position, the element must have 'position: relative/absolute/fixed'. Colour animation needs a plugin such as jQuery Color or jQuery UI.

cards.title: Queues, Chaining & Easing (Part 1)
cards.body: Multiple animate() calls on one element are queued and run one after another: '$("#box").animate({left: 100}).animate({top: 100});'. Properties inside a single call animate simultaneously. Built-in easing: 'swing' (default, slow-fast-slow) and 'linear'.

cards.title: Queues, Chaining & Easing (Part 2)
cards.body: Use 'stop(true, true)' to clear the queue and jump to the end, and callbacks to run code afterward. For simple effects today, CSS transitions are lighter, but animate() remains handy for animating scroll position: '$("html, body").animate({scrollTop: 0}, 600);'.

quiz.question: Which kind of CSS property can jQuery's animate() animate by default?
quiz.explanation: animate() works with numeric values (width, height, opacity, etc.). Colours need an extra plugin.

modules.title: AJAX with jQuery
modules.description: Making AJAX calls the jQuery way: $.ajax(), the shorthand methods, form serialization, promises and global handlers.

cards.title: Configuring $.ajax()
cards.body: $.ajax() takes a settings object: '$.ajax({ url: "/api/students", method: "GET", data: {page: 2}, dataType: "json", success: function(res) { ... }, error: function(xhr, status, err) { ... }, complete: function() { ... } });'. 'method' (older alias 'type') sets the HTTP verb, 'data' becomes the query string (GET) or body (POST), and 'dataType' says what response format to expect and parse.

cards.title: Useful Options (Part 1)
cards.body: 'contentType' (request body type; use "application/json" with JSON.stringify(data)), 'headers' (e.g. CSRF token), 'timeout' in ms, 'cache: false' (adds a timestamp to avoid cached GETs), 'beforeSend' (runs before sending; show a spinner or set headers), 'async', 'processData', and 'xhrFields: {withCredentials: true}' for cross-origin cookies.

cards.title: Useful Options (Part 2)
cards.body: 'complete' runs after success or error and is ideal for hiding a spinner.

quiz.question: Which $.ajax() option runs a function only when the request fails?
quiz.explanation: error runs on failure, success on success, complete on both, and beforeSend before the request is sent.

cards.title: load(), $.get() and $.post()
cards.body: '$("#box").load("page.html")' fetches HTML and places it inside the element ('page.html #section' loads only a part). '$.get(url, data, callback, dataType)' and '$.post(url, data, callback, dataType)' are shortcuts for GET and POST requests: '$.post("/save", {name: "Asha"}, function(res) { alert(res.message); });'.

cards.title: $.getJSON() and $.getScript()
cards.body: '$.getJSON(url, data, callback)' is a GET that expects JSON and returns the parsed result: '$.getJSON("/api/cities", function(list) { ... });'. '$.getScript(url)' loads and runs a JavaScript file on demand, useful for loading plugins only when needed.

cards.title: Serializing Forms
cards.body: '$("form").serialize()' converts all successful form controls into a query string ('name=Asha&age=21') and 'serializeArray()' returns an array of {name, value} objects. Typical submit handler: '$("#f").on("submit", function(e) { e.preventDefault(); $.post("/save", $(this).serialize(), function(r) { ... }); });'. Disabled controls and unchecked checkboxes are not included.

quiz.question: Which jQuery method turns all the fields of a form into a URL-encoded query string?
quiz.explanation: serialize() produces name=value pairs joined with &, ready to send as the request data.

cards.title: done(), fail() and always()
cards.body: $.ajax() and its shorthands return a jqXHR object that works like a promise: '$.ajax(url).done(function(data) { ... }).fail(function(xhr) { ... }).always(function() { ... });'. This is cleaner than callbacks in the settings object and allows several handlers. Note: the old jqXHR '.success()', '.error()' and '.complete()' methods were removed in jQuery 3; use done, fail and always instead.

cards.title: $.when() and Parallel Requests
cards.body: '$.when(req1, req2).done(function(r1, r2) { ... })' runs code after several requests finish (each result is an array [data, status, jqXHR]). In jQuery 3 the deferreds are Promises/A+ compatible, so you can also use 'Promise.all' or async/await with them.

cards.title: Global AJAX Settings & Events
cards.body: '$.ajaxSetup({ timeout: 5000, headers: {...} })' sets defaults for all later requests. Global events fire for every AJAX call: 'ajaxStart' and 'ajaxStop' (ideal for a page-wide loading spinner), 'ajaxSend', 'ajaxSuccess', 'ajaxError' and 'ajaxComplete': '$(document).ajaxStart(function() { $("#spin").show(); }).ajaxStop(function() { $("#spin").hide(); });'.

quiz.question: Which jqXHR method runs after a request finishes whether it succeeded or failed?
quiz.explanation: always() runs on both success and failure, like finally for promises.

cards.title: Rendering JSON as HTML
cards.body: Loop through the data and build elements: '$.getJSON("/api/students", function(list) { var ul = $("#list").empty(); $.each(list, function(i, s) { ul.append($("<li>").text(s.name + " (" + s.marks + ")")); }); });'. Creating elements with '$("<li>").text()' escapes user data automatically, whereas string concatenation with html() is vulnerable to XSS.

cards.title: Loading States & Error Messages
cards.body: Good AJAX UIs show feedback: display a spinner in beforeSend, hide it in always, and show a friendly message in fail (for example 'Could not load data. Try again.' with a retry button). Disable the submit button during the request to prevent duplicate submissions, and show empty-state text when the list comes back empty.

cards.title: Parsing JSON Safely
cards.body: With dataType: 'json' (or $.getJSON) jQuery parses the response for you. When you have a string, use the native 'JSON.parse(str)' inside try/catch; 'jQuery.parseJSON()' has been deprecated since jQuery 3.0. If the server sends the wrong Content-Type or invalid JSON, jQuery calls the error handler with 'parsererror'.

quiz.question: What is the safest way to display a user-supplied name inside a new list item with jQuery?
quiz.explanation: text() inserts the value as plain text, so any HTML or script in the name is not executed.

modules.title: AJAX & jQuery with Django: Practice & Best Practices
modules.description: Connecting browser-side AJAX to Django views, handling CSRF, building small real features, and following good security and performance habits.

cards.title: Returning JSON with JsonResponse
cards.body: A Django view for AJAX returns data instead of a template: 'from django.http import JsonResponse' then 'def students(request): data = list(Student.objects.values("id", "name", "marks")); return JsonResponse({"students": data})'. Use 'safe=False' to return a list directly. Map it in urls.py ('path("api/students/", views.students)') and call it with $.getJSON or fetch.

cards.title: Detecting AJAX & Reading Data (Part 1)
cards.body: GET parameters come from 'request.GET.get("q")', form-style POST data from 'request.POST', and JSON bodies from 'json.loads(request.body)'.

cards.title: Detecting AJAX & Reading Data (Part 2)
cards.body: jQuery adds the header 'X-Requested-With: XMLHttpRequest' to same-origin requests, which you can check with 'request.headers.get("X-Requested-With")'; the old 'request.is_ajax()' was removed in Django 4.0, and fetch() does not send that header at all.

cards.title: Detecting AJAX & Reading Data (Part 3)
cards.body: Return proper status codes, for example 'JsonResponse({...}, status=400)' for invalid input.

cards.title: Returning HTML Partials
