cards.body: Instead of JSON, a view can render a small template and return it: 'return render(request, "partials/rows.html", {"students": qs})'. On the client, '$("#table-body").html(response)' or '.load()' swaps it in. This keeps rendering logic in Django templates and is a simple approach for lists, tables and search results.

quiz.question: Which Django class returns a dictionary as a JSON HTTP response?
quiz.explanation: JsonResponse serializes a dict (or list with safe=False) to JSON and sets the application/json content type.

lessons.title: CSRF Protection for AJAX in Django

cards.title: Why Django Blocks Your POST (Part 1)
cards.body: Django's CsrfViewMiddleware rejects unsafe requests (POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE) that lack a valid CSRF token, returning 403 Forbidden. For AJAX you must send the token yourself.

cards.title: Why Django Blocks Your POST (Part 2)
cards.body: Never use @csrf_exempt just to make the error disappear, as it removes protection. The token is available in the 'csrftoken' cookie and via the '{% csrf_token %}' template tag, which renders a hidden 'csrfmiddlewaretoken' input.

cards.title: Sending the Token with jQuery (Part 1)
cards.body: Read the token and send it in the 'X-CSRFToken' header for every unsafe request: '$.ajaxSetup({ beforeSend: function(xhr, settings) { if (!/^(GET|HEAD|OPTIONS)$/i.test(settings.type) && !this.crossDomain) { xhr.setRequestHeader("X-CSRFToken", csrftoken); } } });'.

cards.title: Sending the Token with jQuery (Part 2)
cards.body: Alternatively include 'csrfmiddlewaretoken' in the form data: '$(form).serialize()' already includes it when the form has {% csrf_token %}.

cards.title: Sending the Token with fetch()
cards.body: 'fetch("/api/save/", { method: "POST", headers: {"Content-Type": "application/json", "X-CSRFToken": csrftoken}, credentials: "same-origin", body: JSON.stringify(data) })'. Get the value from the cookie with a small helper, or place it in the template once: 'const csrftoken = "{{ csrf_token }}";'. If the cookie is not set (the page has no form), decorate the view with '@ensure_csrf_cookie'.

quiz.question: In which HTTP header should an AJAX POST send Django's CSRF token?
quiz.explanation: Django checks the X-CSRFToken header (or the csrfmiddlewaretoken form field) against the CSRF cookie.

lessons.title: Mini Projects: Live Search & Username Check

cards.title: Live Search
cards.body: HTML: 'input#q' and 'tbody#rows'. jQuery: '$("#q").on("input", function() { clearTimeout(t); t = setTimeout(() => { $.get("/search/", {q: $("#q").val()}, function(html) { $("#rows").html(html); }); }, 300); });'. Django view: filter with 'Student.objects.filter(name__icontains=q)[:20]' and render a partial. The 300 ms debounce keeps server load low.

cards.title: Username Availability Check
cards.body: On the blur or input event of the username field, call '$.getJSON("/check-username/", {u: value})'. Django view: 'return JsonResponse({"taken": User.objects.filter(username__iexact=u).exists()})'. Show 'Username taken' in red or 'Available' in green with '.text()' and a CSS class. Always repeat the uniqueness check in the final form validation, since the AJAX check is only a convenience.

cards.title: Delete with Confirmation
cards.body: Use delegation: '$("#rows").on("click", ".del", function() { var row = $(this).closest("tr"); if (confirm("Delete?")) { $.post("/delete/" + row.data("id") + "/").done(function() { row.fadeOut(300, function() { $(this).remove(); }); }).fail(function() { alert("Could not delete"); }); } });'. The row disappears only after the server confirms success, and the CSRF header is added by ajaxSetup.

quiz.question: Why must the username-uniqueness check also be done on the server when the form is finally submitted?
options: The AJAX check is only a convenience and can be bypassed or become stale
quiz.explanation: Client-side checks can be skipped or change between check and submit, so the server must always enforce rules.

cards.title: Security Checklist (Part 1)
cards.body: Always validate and authorize on the server (check the user may perform the action). Protect unsafe methods with CSRF tokens. Prevent XSS by inserting untrusted data with text()/textContent rather than html()/innerHTML, and by letting Django templates auto-escape.

cards.title: Security Checklist (Part 2)
cards.body: Use HTTPS, avoid putting secrets in JavaScript, and return generic error messages instead of stack traces. Configure CORS narrowly (specific origins) if a separate front-end calls your API.

cards.title: Performance Tips
cards.body: Cache selectors in variables ('var $list = $("#list");'), use event delegation instead of many handlers, debounce rapid events, abort outdated requests, paginate large lists, and request only the fields you need. Combine requests where possible, and minimise DOM updates by building HTML once and inserting it in a single call.

cards.title: jQuery vs Vanilla JS & Good Habits (Part 1)
cards.body: Modern JavaScript can replace most jQuery: 'document.querySelectorAll', 'classList', 'addEventListener', 'fetch' and 'animate' via CSS. Choose jQuery when maintaining existing code or using jQuery plugins; prefer vanilla JS in new, small projects.

cards.title: jQuery vs Vanilla JS & Good Habits (Part 2)
cards.body: Always handle loading and failure states, keep AJAX code out of HTML attributes, name functions clearly, and keep the page usable (progressive enhancement) when JavaScript fails.

quiz.question: Which approach is safest for showing user-generated content returned by an AJAX call?
options: Insert it inside a script tag
quiz.explanation: text() and textContent treat the value as plain text, so injected HTML or scripts are not executed.

units.title: Module 10: Django
units.description: Build web apps with Django — projects and apps, views and URLs, templates, static files, models, admin, forms, validation and deployment.

modules.title: Django Basics
modules.description: What a framework is, what Django is, the MVT pattern, and how to set Django up.

cards.title: What is a Framework?
cards.body: A framework is ready-made structure and tools for building software. Like using a khichdi recipe instead of inventing one — you follow the guideline and save time.

cards.title: Why Use a Framework?
cards.body: No need to start from scratch. It saves time, improves productivity, gives clean and reusable code, and makes testing and debugging easier.

cards.title: Web Frameworks
cards.body: A web framework helps build web apps (templates, database access, APIs). Examples: Django, Flask, Laravel, CodeIgniter, Express JS, Spring.

quiz.question: What is the main purpose of a framework?
options: To remove the need for a database
To make websites slower but safer
To save time by providing ready-made structure and tools
quiz.explanation: Frameworks let developers focus on their unique features instead of writing common code again.

cards.title: What is Django?
cards.body: Django is a free, open-source, high-level Python web framework. It follows the MVT pattern. Created in 2003 at Lawrence Journal-World newspaper, released publicly in July 2005 (BSD license).

cards.title: Why Django?
cards.body: Fast, secure, scalable and open source. It has built-in authentication, a development server and SQLite database. Used by YouTube, Instagram, Spotify, NASA and more.

quiz.question: Django is written in which language?
quiz.explanation: Django is a Python-based web framework.

cards.title: Model, View, Template
cards.body:
MVT splits an app into 3 parts:
Model → handles the database (data layer)
View → handles requests and logic
Template → what the user sees (HTML/CSS/JS + DTL)

cards.title: How a Request Flows
cards.body:
User → URL → View → (Model ↔ Database) → View → Template → response to user.
The View is the middle person between Model and Template.

cards.title: Why MVT?
cards.body: Organized code, independent parts, less complexity, and easy to maintain and modify.

quiz.question: Which MVT part talks to the database?
quiz.explanation: The Model is the data access layer; the View asks it for data.

cards.title: Requirements
cards.body:
Python 3 or higher, PIP, a code editor (VS Code, PyCharm...) and a web browser.
Check: python --version and pip --version

cards.title: Install Django
cards.body:
pip install django
Specific version: pip install django==3.2
Uninstall: pip uninstall django
Check: django-admin --version

cards.title: Virtual Environment (Recommended)
cards.body:
Keeps each project's packages separate:
python -m venv project1
project1\Scripts\activate (Windows)
python -m pip install Django

quiz.question: Which command installs Django?
quiz.explanation: Django is installed from PyPI using pip.

modules.title: Django Project & Apps
modules.description: Create a project, understand its files, run the server and add applications.

cards.title: Project vs App
cards.body: A project is the whole website. An app is one part of it. Example: SchoolProject has Registration, Fees, Exam and Result apps.

cards.title: startproject
cards.body:
django-admin startproject schoolproject
Creates the project folder with manage.py and an inner folder holding __init__.py, settings.py, urls.py, asgi.py and wsgi.py.

quiz.question: Which command creates a new Django project?
quiz.explanation: startproject builds the project folder structure.

cards.title: manage.py, __init__.py, wsgi/asgi
cards.body:
manage.py → command-line tool to run commands.
__init__.py → makes the folder a Python package.
wsgi.py / asgi.py → connect the project to a web server.

cards.title: settings.py
cards.body:
Main configuration file:
DEBUG = True → shows detailed errors (use False in production)
INSTALLED_APPS → enabled apps
TEMPLATES → template settings
DATABASES → database (SQLite by default)

cards.title: urls.py
cards.body:
Maps URLs to views. By default it has only the admin URL:
urlpatterns = [ path('admin/', admin.site.urls) ]

quiz.question: Where do you install a new app?
quiz.explanation: An app works only after its name is added to INSTALLED_APPS.

cards.title: runserver
cards.body:
Inside the project folder run:
python manage.py runserver
Open http://127.0.0.1:8000 or http://localhost:8000.
Custom port: python manage.py runserver 8080

cards.title: Stop the Server
cards.body: Press Ctrl + C. Restart the server if some changes (like settings) do not show up.

quiz.question: How do you stop the Django development server?
quiz.explanation: Ctrl + C stops the running process in the terminal.

cards.title: startapp
cards.body:
Inside the project folder:
python manage.py startapp course
You can create many apps (course, fees, result...) one by one.

cards.title: Install the App
cards.body:
Creating is not enough — add the app name in settings.py:
INSTALLED_APPS = ['django.contrib.admin', ..., 'course']

cards.title: App Folder Files
cards.body:
migrations/ → database change files
admin.py → register models for admin
models.py → database tables
views.py → view functions
tests.py → tests
apps.py → app configuration

quiz.question: Which file holds the view functions of an app?
quiz.explanation: views.py is where request-handling functions are written.

modules.title: Views & URLs
modules.description: Write view functions and connect them to URLs.

cards.title: What is a View?
cards.body: A view is a Python function that takes a request and returns a response (HTML, redirect, 404, image...). Views can be function-based or class-based.

cards.title: First View

quiz.question: What does a view function return?
quiz.explanation: Every view must return a response for the browser.

cards.title: Mapping URL to View
cards.body:
urls.py connects URL paths to view functions:
from course import views
urlpatterns = [
    path('learndj/', views.learn_django),
]
Visit /learndj/ to see the result.

cards.title: path() Arguments
cards.body:
path(route, view, kwargs=None, name=None)
route → URL pattern
view → function to call
kwargs → extra data (optional)
name → name to refer to this URL

cards.title: Many URLs, One View
cards.body:
path('learndj/', views.learn_django)
path('altlearndj/', views.learn_django)
Both URLs open the same view.

quiz.question: Which path() argument gives a URL a reusable name?
quiz.explanation: The name lets you refer to the URL later (e.g. with {% url %}).

cards.title: Views in Two Apps
cards.body:
Each app has its own views.py. If function names or modules clash, use an alias:
from course import views as cv
from fees import views as fv

cards.title: Direct Import
cards.body:
Or import the functions directly:
from course.views import learn_django
from fees.views import fees_django
path('feesdj/', fees_django)

quiz.question: Why use 'import views as cv'?
options: To avoid name clashes between apps
quiz.explanation: Two apps can both have 'views'; an alias keeps them separate.

cards.title: Why App URLs?
cards.body: Writing every URL in the project urls.py makes apps depend on the project. Giving each app its own urls.py makes apps independent and reusable.

cards.title: Using include()
cards.body:
course/urls.py
urlpatterns = [ path('learndj/', views.learn_django) ]

Project urls.py
from django.urls import path, include
path('cor/', include('course.urls'))
URL: /cor/learndj

quiz.question: What does include('course.urls') do?
options: Brings the app's URL patterns into the project urls.py
quiz.explanation: include() links an app's urls.py to the project under a prefix.

modules.title: Templates & Django Template Language
modules.description: Show HTML pages and pass dynamic data using the Django Template Language (DTL).

cards.title: What is a Template?
cards.body: A template is a text file (usually HTML) with variables and tags. Business logic stays in views.py; presentation stays in templates.

cards.title: Set Up Templates
cards.body:
Create a templates folder in the project root. In settings.py:
TEMPLATES_DIR = BASE_DIR / 'templates'
TEMPLATES = [{ 'DIRS': [TEMPLATES_DIR], ... }]
(Django 3.0 and older: os.path.join(BASE_DIR, 'templates'))

cards.title: render()

quiz.question: Which function loads a template and returns a response?
quiz.explanation: render(request, template_name, context) does this job.

cards.title: Folder per App
cards.body:
Inside templates, keep one folder per app:
templates/course/courseone.html
templates/fees/feesone.html
Then use render(request, 'course/courseone.html'). Naming by app is a convention.

cards.title: Templates Inside an App
cards.body: You can also keep templates/ inside each app. Set 'DIRS': [] and 'APP_DIRS': True, and make sure the app is in INSTALLED_APPS.

quiz.question: Which setting lets Django find templates inside apps?
quiz.explanation: APP_DIRS tells Django to look for a templates folder in every installed app.

cards.title: Send Data (context)
Show Data with {{ }}
cards.body:
In the template:

Hello {{nm}}

Duration: {{du}}, Seats: {{st}}

Variables may contain letters, digits and underscores, but no spaces or punctuation.

quiz.question: How do you print a variable 'nm' in a template?
quiz.explanation: Double curly braces output a variable's value.

cards.title: Using Filters
Date & Time Filters
cards.body:
{{ value|date:'D d M Y' }} → Fri 09 Feb 2020
{{ value|time:'H:i' }} → 22:30
Common codes: d day, m month, M Jan, Y 4-digit year, H 24-hour, i minutes.

cards.title: floatformat
cards.body:
{{ 34.23234|floatformat }} → 34.2
{{ 34.23234|floatformat:3 }} → 34.232
{{ 34.5|floatformat:0 }} → 34 (or 35)
Rounds numbers for display.

quiz.question: Which symbol applies a filter in a template?
quiz.explanation: Syntax is {{ variable|filter }}.

cards.title: if Tag
else & elif

quiz.question: Which tag ends an if block?
quiz.explanation: Every {% if %} needs a matching {% endif %}.

cards.title: for Tag
cards.body:
{% for stu in student %}
  • {{ stu }}
    • {% endfor %}
Use {% empty %} to show text when the list is empty.

cards.title: forloop Variables
cards.body:
forloop.counter → 1, 2, 3...
forloop.counter0 → 0, 1, 2...
forloop.revcounter → counts down
forloop.first / forloop.last → True on first / last item

cards.title: Dot Lookup
cards.body: {{ stu.name }} — Django tries in order: dictionary lookup, attribute/method lookup, then list index (e.g. {{ list.0 }}).

quiz.question: Which variable gives the loop count starting from 1?
quiz.explanation: counter starts at 1; counter0 starts at 0.

modules.title: Static Files & Template Inheritance
modules.description: Use CSS, JS and images, reuse page layouts, and link pages together.

cards.title: What are Static Files?
cards.body: CSS, JavaScript, images and videos are static files. Create a static folder in the project root with sub-folders like css, js and images.

cards.title: settings.py for Static
cards.body:
STATIC_URL = '/static/'
STATIC_DIR = BASE_DIR / 'static'
STATICFILES_DIRS = [STATIC_DIR]
Static folders can also be inside each app (app/static/).

cards.title: Use in a Template

quiz.question: Which tag must be written before using {% static %}?
quiz.explanation: load static makes the static tag available in the template.

cards.title: Base & Child Templates
extends & block
Rules
cards.body:
{% extends %} must be the first tag in the template.
Use more blocks in the base template.
A child need not fill every block.
Do not repeat a block name in one template.

quiz.question: Where must the {% extends %} tag be written?
quiz.explanation: Inheritance does not work if extends is not first.

cards.title: url Tag
cards.body: Give the URL a name: path('about/', views.about, name='aboutus') Then link with: About If the URL changes, links stay correct.

cards.title: include Tag

quiz.question: Why use {% url 'aboutus' %} instead of a fixed link?
options: The link updates automatically if the URL pattern changes
It hides the page from users
quiz.explanation: Named URLs avoid broken links when route paths change.

modules.title: Models & ORM
modules.description: Create database tables using Python classes — no SQL needed.

cards.title: What is an ORM?
cards.body: ORM (Object Relational Mapper) lets Python code talk to databases (SQLite, MySQL, PostgreSQL, Oracle). A class becomes a table, an object becomes a row.

cards.title: Create a Model
cards.body:
models.py
class Student(models.Model):
    stuid = models.IntegerField()
    stuname = models.CharField(max_length=70)
    stuemail = models.EmailField(max_length=70)
Each attribute is a column.

quiz.question: In Django ORM, a model class represents:
quiz.explanation: Each model usually maps to one table; each attribute is a column.

cards.title: Common Field Types
cards.body:
IntegerField → numbers
CharField → short text (max_length required)
TextField → long text
EmailField, URLField → validated text
BooleanField → True/False
DateField → date
AutoField → auto-increment id

cards.title: Field Options
cards.body:
null=True → store empty as NULL
default='Not Available' → default value
primary_key=True → makes it the primary key
unique=True → no duplicate values
If no primary key is set, Django adds an auto 'id'.

quiz.question: Which CharField argument is required?
quiz.explanation: CharField must know the maximum length of the text.

cards.title: makemigrations & migrate
cards.body:
1. Add the app to INSTALLED_APPS
2. python manage.py makemigrations → creates a migration file (SQL plan)
3. python manage.py migrate → creates/updates the tables
Run both again after any model change.

cards.title: See the SQL
cards.body:
python manage.py sqlmigrate enroll 0001
Shows the SQL for migration 0001 of the 'enroll' app. Migration files are saved in the app's migrations folder.

quiz.question: Which command actually creates the tables in the database?
quiz.explanation: makemigrations only prepares the plan; migrate applies it.

cards.title: QuerySet & all()
cards.body: A QuerySet is a list of objects from the database. Student.objects.all() returns every row of the table. You can also filter and order QuerySets.

cards.title: View + Template

quiz.question: Which code gets all records of the Student model?
quiz.explanation: The model's objects manager has the all() method.

modules.title: Django Admin
modules.description: Manage your database through Django's built-in admin panel.

cards.title: What is Admin?
cards.body: A built-in app that gives a ready admin panel for create, read, update and delete (CRUD) on your tables without writing SQL. Open it at /admin/.

cards.title: Create Superuser
cards.body:
python manage.py createsuperuser
Enter username, email and password, then log in at http://127.0.0.1:8000/admin/ (run migrate first).

cards.title: Register a Model
cards.body:
admin.py
from django.contrib import admin
from .models import Student
admin.site.register(Student)
Now the Student table shows in the admin panel.

quiz.question: Which file is used to register models in the admin panel?
quiz.explanation: Models are registered in the app's admin.py.

cards.title: __str__() Method
ModelAdmin & list_display
cards.body:
class StudentAdmin(admin.ModelAdmin):
    list_display = ('id', 'stuname', 'stuemail')
admin.site.register(Student, StudentAdmin)
Shows chosen columns in the list page. A decorator also works: @admin.register(Student)

quiz.question: What does list_display control?
options: Which columns show on the admin list page
quiz.explanation: list_display chooses the fields shown in the change list.

modules.title: Django Forms
modules.description: Build forms with Python, show them in templates, and validate user input.

cards.title: Create a Form Class
cards.body:
forms.py (inside the app)
from django import forms
class StudentRegistration(forms.Form):
    name = forms.CharField()
    email = forms.EmailField()
Django turns it into HTML and validates the data.

cards.title: Show the Form
cards.body:
views.py
fm = StudentRegistration()
return render(request, 'enroll/userregistration.html', {'form': fm})

Template:
<form action='' method='post'>{% csrf_token %}{{ form.as_p }}<input type='submit'></form>
Form tag and submit button must be written by you.

cards.title: Bound & Unbound Forms
cards.body:
Unbound = empty form, cannot validate.
Bound = form with data (e.g. StudentRegistration(request.POST)); it can validate and show the data.

quiz.question: Does {{ form }} add the <form> tag and submit button?
options: No, you must add them yourself
quiz.explanation: {{ form }} renders only the fields.

cards.title: Render the Whole Form
cards.body:
{{ form }} → all fields {{ form.as_p }} → each field in

{{ form.as_table }} → table rows (add yourself) {{ form.as_ul }} → list items (add
    yourself)

cards.title: Render Fields Manually
cards.body:
{{ form.name }} → input
{{ form.name.label_tag }} → label
{{ form.name.value }} → value
{{ form.name.errors }} → errors
Or loop: {% for field in form %} {{ field.label_tag }} {{ field }} {% endfor %}

quiz.question:
Which option wraps each field in a

tag?
quiz.explanation: as_p puts each label and field inside a paragraph.

cards.title: Common Form Fields
cards.body: CharField, IntegerField, DecimalField, FloatField, BooleanField, EmailField, URLField, DateField, TimeField, DateTimeField, FileField, ImageField, ChoiceField, MultipleChoiceField, SlugField, RegexField.

cards.title: Field Arguments
cards.body:
required=True → must be filled (default True)
label='Your Name' → label text
initial='Rahul' → starting value
help_text='Enter full name' → hint text
error_messages={'required': 'Please enter name'} → custom errors

quiz.question: What is the default value of 'required' in a form field?
quiz.explanation: Fields are required unless you set required=False.

cards.title: What is a Widget?
cards.body:
A widget is Django's HTML input element. It renders the HTML and reads the submitted data.
password = forms.CharField(widget=forms.PasswordInput)

cards.title: Common Widgets & attrs
cards.body:
TextInput, NumberInput, EmailInput, PasswordInput, HiddenInput, DateInput, Select, CheckboxSelectMultiple, FileInput.
Add HTML attributes with attrs:
forms.TextInput(attrs={'class': 'myclass', 'placeholder': 'Name'})

quiz.question: How do you add a CSS class to a form widget?
quiz.explanation: widget=forms.TextInput(attrs={'class': '...'}) sets HTML attributes.

cards.title: GET vs POST
cards.body:
GET → for requests that do not change anything (e.g. search); data shows in the URL.
POST → for requests that change data (e.g. registration, passwords); data is hidden from the URL.

cards.title: What is CSRF?
cards.body: Cross-Site Request Forgery: a malicious site makes a visitor's browser send a request to your site, and your server thinks the user made it.

cards.title: csrf_token
cards.body: Add {% csrf_token %} inside every POST form. Django adds a hidden random token and rejects requests without a valid one.

quiz.question: Which tag protects a POST form from CSRF?
quiz.explanation: csrf_token adds a hidden security token to the form.

cards.title: is_valid() & cleaned_data
Validate One Field
Validate Whole Form
Built-in & Custom Validators
cards.body:
Built-in: from django.core import validators
name = forms.CharField(validators=[validators.MaxLengthValidator(10)])
Custom: write a function that raises forms.ValidationError and pass it in validators=[my_function].

quiz.question: Which method checks one specific field called 'email'?
quiz.explanation: clean_<fieldname>() validates a single field; clean() validates the whole form.

modules.title: Deployment
modules.description: Put your Django project online.

cards.title: Prepare the Project
cards.body:
1. pip freeze > req.txt (list of packages)
2. Add STATIC_ROOT = os.path.join(BASE_DIR, 'static/')
3. Set DEBUG = False and add your domain to ALLOWED_HOSTS
4. Zip the project and upload it to PythonAnywhere.

cards.title: Set Up on the Server
cards.body:
Open a Bash console:
mkvirtualenv envname --python=/usr/bin/python3.8
Unzip the project, then: pip install -r req.txt
In the Web tab, create a web app and edit wsgi.py so it points to your project's settings.

cards.title: Static Files & Go Live
cards.body:
python manage.py collectstatic
In the Web tab → Static Files, add URL (/static/) and the directory path. Click Reload to publish the site.

quiz.question: Which command gathers all static files into STATIC_ROOT for deployment?
quiz.explanation: collectstatic copies all static files into one folder for the web server.

units.title: Module 11: Practice Questions — Web & Programming Basics
units.description: Quick MCQ practice for HTML, CSS with Bootstrap, JavaScript, Python basics and Python OOP.

modules.title: HTML Practice Questions
modules.description: 50 MCQs on tags, forms, tables, semantic HTML and page structure.

quiz.question: What kind of language is HTML?
quiz.explanation: HTML is a markup language: it uses tags to structure the content of web pages. It is not a programming language, and styling is done with CSS.

quizzes.question: What kind of language is HTML?
quizzes.explanation: HTML is a markup language: it uses tags to structure the content of web pages. It is not a programming language, and styling is done with CSS.

quizzes.question: What is <!DOCTYPE html> used for?
options: It adds a comment to the page
